arXiv:2611.03289v1 [cs.AI] 02 Nov 2026

Top-kk Retrieval Leaves
Memory Value Undetermined

Arman Behnam Department of Computer Science Illinois Institute of Technology Chicago, IL, USA abehnam@hawk.illinoistech.edu
Abstract

A memory-augmented agent must decide which memories to keep, merge and retrieve, and its only evidence of their value is its retrieval log: the memories it retrieved in each episode and whether it succeeded. Existing methods assign every memory a value from this log, even when the log cannot separate one memory’s contribution from another’s. We treat the log as an experiment that nobody designed and ask which memory values it determines. Two counts answer this before any outcome is observed: how often each memory was retrieved, and how often each pair was retrieved together. From these counts, we prove that top-kk retrieval leaves every memory value undetermined, however many episodes are logged, and that a question with its own memories, asked once, determines at most one of their values. On fourteen standard memory benchmarks, no memory value is determined in any of 5555 configurations. Both causes are choices about retrieval. We introduce LEDGER, which estimates each determined Shapley value in closed form with a confidence interval and reports every other value as undetermined. It merges memories with identical histories without losing a determined value, and it retrieves so that the next log determines more. On pooled HotpotQA, LEDGER raises the fraction of memories determined from 0.0010.001 to 0.7970.797, at a cost of 2.62.6 accuracy points on HotpotQA and with a gain of 2.72.7 on LoCoMo. Code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ledger-review-AF71/.

1 Introduction

Agents that operate over long horizons keep a store of memories and must decide which to retain, which to merge and which to retrieve for each query (Pink et al., 2025; Du et al., 2025). Each of these decisions depends on how much every memory contributes to the agent’s success. A deployed agent can learn this only from its own history: in each episode it retrieved some memories and then succeeded or failed. This paper asks what that history can tell us about the value of each memory, and when it can tell us nothing.

Existing systems follow three approaches. The first scores memories with proxies such as recency, access frequency or similarity to the query (Wei et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2026b). The second learns a value signal from downstream reward (Tan et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026). The third computes the Shapley value (Shapley, 1953), which divides the agent’s success fairly among the memories it used (Wei et al., 2026b; Ye and Yoganarasimhan, 2025; Patel et al., 2025). Three challenges stand in the way. First, a deployed agent cannot experiment on its memory: Shapley methods need outcomes for sets of memories that were never retrieved together, and the agent cannot go back and retrieve them. Second, memories are retrieved in groups, so the history may not separate the contribution of one memory from that of another. When it does not, a method still returns a number, but the number is set by the method and not by the data, and nothing in the output reveals this. Third, making the history more informative can lower accuracy, because it means changing what the agent retrieves.

We treat the history as an experiment that nobody designed. Each episode is a trial in which a set of memories was retrieved and an outcome was observed, and the theory of experimental design states which quantities a set of trials determines (Rao, 1973; Pukelsheim, 2006). This view answers each challenge. First, it needs no new trials, because it asks only what the recorded ones determine. Second, it decides, for every memory, whether the history determines its value before any value is estimated, so a method can decline to report a value that the data do not support. Third, it identifies which changes to retrieval make the history informative, so their cost in accuracy can be measured.

The analysis needs only two counts that any retrieval log contains: how often each memory was retrieved, and how often each pair was retrieved together. From these counts alone, before any outcome is used, it decides which memory values the history determines. Applied to standard memory benchmarks (Yang et al., 2018; Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025), it finds that none is determined. One common convention is enough to cause this: retrieving the same number of memories for every query. A second, giving each question its own memories, limits each question to as many determined values as it has episodes. Both conventions are choices about retrieval, so the remedy changes retrieval: share one store across queries, vary how many memories are retrieved, and fill part of each retrieval with the relevant memories retrieved least often. On pooled HotpotQA most values then become determined, fewer on other stores, while accuracy falls slightly on one corpus and rises on another. Our method, LEDGER, estimates the determined values with confidence intervals and reports the rest as undetermined.

Figure 1 shows the first convention on four memories. Each pair is retrieved once, giving six episodes for four unknown values, which looks sufficient. Yet every episode retrieves two memories, so adding the same amount to every value and removing twice that amount from the baseline leaves every predicted outcome unchanged: the history fixes only the differences between values. One episode of size one and one of size three determine all four. Appendix H discusses the scope, applications and limitations of these results, and Appendix I collects the notation and terms.

This paper makes three contributions. First, it answers a question that prior work leaves open: which memory values a deployed agent’s history determines. Proxy and learned methods report values without asking it, and Shapley methods avoid it by replaying sets of memories; we answer it exactly from the history, and show that a fixed retrieval size leaves every value undetermined however long the history grows (Section 3). Second, it gives LEDGER, which computes each determined value in closed form with a confidence interval, reports every other value as undetermined, and merges memories with identical histories without losing any determined value (Section 4). Third, it shows that the conventions the field uses to evaluate memory leave every memory value undetermined, and that changing how memories are retrieved makes most values determined on pooled HotpotQA and fewer on other stores, at a measured cost in accuracy (Sections 4 and 5). The same counts appear in slate off-policy evaluation, which sets the undetermined part aside because it does not affect the value of a policy (Swaminathan et al., 2017); for memory, the undetermined part is the finding.

2 Background and Problem Formulation

Preliminaries.

We use three concepts from prior work. Möbius dividends: every set function vv on the subsets of [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\{1,\dots,n\} can be written uniquely as v⁡(S)=∑B⊆SθBv(S)=\sum_{B\subseteq S}\theta_{B}, where the dividend θB\theta_{B} is the part of the value that the set BB creates jointly and none of its proper subsets creates (Harsanyi, 1963; Grabisch et al., 2000). The Shapley value of element ii is the unique attribution satisfying efficiency, symmetry, null player and additivity (Shapley, 1953); in dividends it is φi=∑B∋iθB/|B|\varphi_{i}=\sum_{B\ni i}\theta_{B}/|B|, so each dividend is shared equally among its members (Harsanyi, 1963). Estimability: in a linear model 𝐫=𝐀​𝜷+𝜺\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{A}\bm{\beta}+\bm{\varepsilon}, a combination 𝐜⊤​𝜷\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\bm{\beta} is estimable when some linear function of 𝐫\mathbf{r} has expectation 𝐜⊤​𝜷\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\bm{\beta} for every 𝜷\bm{\beta}, which holds exactly when 𝐜\mathbf{c} lies in the row space of 𝐀\mathbf{A} (Rao, 1973, Section 4a.2); otherwise all least-squares solutions fit the data equally well and give 𝐜⊤​𝜷\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\bm{\beta} every real value (Lemma A.2). Appendices A.1 and A.2 state these concepts formally.

Setting.

An agent holds a store of nn memories m1,…,mnm_{1},\dots,m_{n}, identified with [n][n]. In episode t∈[T]t\in[T] it receives a query qtq_{t} drawn from a distribution 𝒟Q\mathcal{D}_{Q}, retrieves a non-empty set St⊆[n]S_{t}\subseteq[n], answers, and observes an outcome rt∈[0,1]r_{t}\in[0,1], for example whether the answer was correct. We make two assumptions; Appendix A.3 discusses what each requires and what is lost when it fails.

Assumption 1 (Outcome model).

For each query qq there is a set function vq:2[n]→[0,1]v_{q}:2^{[n]}\to[0,1] such that 𝔼[rt∣ℱt−1,qt,St]=vqt(St)\mathbb{E}[r_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1},q_{t},S_{t}]=v_{q_{t}}(S_{t}), where ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1} is the history before episode tt, and ηt=rt−vqt​(St)\eta_{t}=r_{t}-v_{q_{t}}(S_{t}) is conditionally σ\sigma-sub Gaussian.

Assumption 2 (Resolution dd).

The query-averaged value v⁡(S)=𝔼q∼𝒟Q​[vq​(S)]v(S)=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D}_{Q}}[v_{q}(S)] has θB=0\theta_{B}=0 whenever |B|>d|B|>d.

The baseline θ∅=v⁡(∅)\theta_{\emptyset}=v(\emptyset) is the expected outcome with nothing retrieved, and the value of memory ii is its Shapley value φi\varphi_{i} under vv, which the baseline does not enter.

Input and output.

The method reads only what an agent already records: for each episode tt, the retrieved set StS_{t} and the outcome rtr_{t}. We store the sets as a binary matrix 𝐗∈{0,1}T×n\mathbf{X}\in\{0,1\}^{T\times n}, one row per episode and one column per memory, with 𝐗t​i=1\mathbf{X}_{ti}=1 exactly when mi∈Stm_{i}\in S_{t}, and the outcomes as a vector 𝐫\mathbf{r}. The product 𝐗⊤​𝐗\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}\mathbf{X} holds the two counts of the introduction,

(𝐗⊤​𝐗)i​i=freq⁡(mi),(𝐗⊤​𝐗)i​j=co⁡(mi,mj),\bigl(\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}\mathbf{X}\bigr)_{ii}=\mathrm{freq}(m_{i}),\qquad\bigl(\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}\mathbf{X}\bigr)_{ij}=\mathrm{co}(m_{i},m_{j}), (1)

how often mim_{i} was retrieved and how often mim_{i} and mjm_{j} were retrieved together. By Assumption 2, each outcome is the sum of the dividends of the retrieved sets of at most dd memories plus noise εt=rt−v⁡(St)\varepsilon_{t}=r_{t}-v(S_{t}). This gives the linear model derived in Appendix A.4,

𝐫=𝐗d𝜽+𝜺,(𝐗d)t​B=𝟏[B⊆St],|B|≤d,\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{X}_{d}\bm{\theta}+\bm{\varepsilon},\qquad(\mathbf{X}_{d})_{tB}=\mathbf{1}[B\subseteq S_{t}],\quad|B|\leq d, (2)

whose column for B=∅B=\emptyset is all ones and carries the baseline; at d=1d=1, 𝐗1=[𝟏T∣𝐗]\mathbf{X}_{1}=[\mathbf{1}_{T}\mid\mathbf{X}]. The output has one entry per memory: an estimate of φi\varphi_{i} with a confidence interval when the log determines it, and undetermined otherwise.

Problem.

Given this log, we first ask which memory values it determines. Memory ii is identifiable when the log determines φi\varphi_{i}: writing φi=(𝐜(i))⊤​𝜽\varphi_{i}=(\mathbf{c}^{(i)})^{\!\top}\bm{\theta} with cB(i)=𝟏[i∈B]/|B|c^{(i)}_{B}=\mathbf{1}[i\in B]/|B|, this holds exactly when 𝐜(i)\mathbf{c}^{(i)} lies in the row space of 𝐗d\mathbf{X}_{d} (Definition A.4), and it is decided from 𝐗d\mathbf{X}_{d} alone, before any outcome is seen. The determined values then guide how the agent manages its store: which memories to merge without losing a value, which to keep under a budget (Appendix F.7), and how to retrieve so that the next log determines more, at a cost in accuracy that we measure.

3 What a Top-kk Log Determines

The problem began with one decision for each memory: whether the log determines its value. This section makes that decision for the logs that agents actually produce. It first shows that whether 𝐜(i)\mathbf{c}^{(i)} lies in the row space of 𝐗d\mathbf{X}_{d} depends only on counts the agent already keeps, and then checks this condition under three common retrieval conventions: retrieving a fixed number of memories per query, giving each query its own memories, and retrieving some memories always together. For each convention, it identifies what the log cannot see and the change to retrieval that restores it. All proofs are in Appendix B.

What a log cannot see.

By Section 2, memory ii is identifiable exactly when 𝐜(i)\mathbf{c}^{(i)} lies in the row space of 𝐗d\mathbf{X}_{d}, that is, when it is orthogonal to the kernel ker⁡𝐗d\ker\mathbf{X}_{d}. We call each 𝐡∈ker⁡𝐗d\mathbf{h}\in\ker\mathbf{X}_{d} an invisible change: 𝜽\bm{\theta} and 𝜽+s​𝐡\bm{\theta}+s\mathbf{h} predict the same expected outcome in every episode for every s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}, while φi\varphi_{i} moves by s​(𝐜(i))⊤​𝐡s\,(\mathbf{c}^{(i)})^{\!\top}\mathbf{h}. Hence φi\varphi_{i} is determined exactly when (𝐜(i))⊤​𝐡=0(\mathbf{c}^{(i)})^{\!\top}\mathbf{h}=0 for every 𝐡∈ker⁡𝐗d\mathbf{h}\in\ker\mathbf{X}_{d}. Since ker⁡𝐗d=ker⁡(𝐗d⊤​𝐗d)\ker\mathbf{X}_{d}=\ker(\mathbf{X}_{d}^{\!\top}\mathbf{X}_{d}) (Appendix B.1), the invisible changes depend only on 𝐗d⊤​𝐗d\mathbf{X}_{d}^{\!\top}\mathbf{X}_{d}, which at d=1d=1 is

𝐗1⊤​𝐗1=[T𝐟⊤𝐟𝐗⊤​𝐗],fi=freq⁡(mi).\mathbf{X}_{1}^{\!\top}\mathbf{X}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}T&\mathbf{f}^{\!\top}\\ \mathbf{f}&\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}\mathbf{X}\end{bmatrix},\qquad f_{i}=\mathrm{freq}(m_{i}). (3)

Whether each memory is identifiable is therefore decided by TT, the retrieval frequencies and the co-retrieval counts alone, and at resolution dd by the number of episodes that retrieve each set of at most 2​d2d memories (Lemma B.1). The retrieval convention that produces these counts therefore decides which memory values a log can determine, before any outcome is observed and whatever the memories contain.

A fixed retrieval size.

The most common convention retrieves the kk memories most relevant to the query, so every episode retrieves the same number of memories; we call such a log a top-kk log. In a top-kk log, an episode that retrieves a set BB of fewer than kk memories retrieves exactly k−|B|k-|B| other memories with it. In every episode, therefore, the columns of 𝐗d\mathbf{X}_{d} for the sets B∪{j}B\cup\{j\} with j∉Bj\notin B sum to k−|B|k-|B| times the column for BB, which gives the invisible change

𝐡B=∑j∉B𝐞B∪{j}−(k−|B|)​𝐞B∈ker⁡𝐗d,|B|<d,\mathbf{h}_{B}\;=\;\sum_{j\notin B}\mathbf{e}_{B\cup\{j\}}\;-\;(k-|B|)\,\mathbf{e}_{B}\;\in\;\ker\mathbf{X}_{d},\qquad|B|<d, (4)

where 𝐞B\mathbf{e}_{B} is the unit vector for θB\theta_{B}. For B=∅B=\emptyset, (𝐜(i))⊤​𝐡∅=1(\mathbf{c}^{(i)})^{\!\top}\mathbf{h}_{\emptyset}=1 for every memory ii, so adding 𝐡∅\mathbf{h}_{\emptyset} changes every φi\varphi_{i} without changing any predicted outcome.

Theorem 1 (Top-kk leaves every value undetermined).

If every episode retrieves exactly kk memories, no memory is identifiable, at any resolution dd and any number of episodes TT. If, in addition, outcomes are binary and each vqv_{q} takes values in (0,1)(0,1), no estimator of any φi\varphi_{i} is consistent.

At d=1d=1, the invisible change 𝐡∅\mathbf{h}_{\emptyset} raises every memory’s value by ss and lowers the baseline by k​sks; this is the ambiguity of Figure 1. No estimator is consistent because adding a small multiple of 𝐡∅\mathbf{h}_{\emptyset} to the dividends of every vqv_{q} leaves the distribution of the log unchanged, so two different values of φi\varphi_{i} produce the same data (Appendix B.2). More episodes do not help, because each new episode again retrieves exactly kk memories. The invisible changes disappear only if the retrieval size varies, and the next proposition gives how many sizes are needed.

Proposition 1 (Sizes needed).

If the retrieval sizes take at most dd distinct values, then ker⁡𝐗d\ker\mathbf{X}_{d} contains a nonzero invisible change at every TT.

At least d+1d+1 distinct sizes are therefore needed for the log to determine every dividend; at d=1d=1, two. With at most dd sizes, all below n/2n/2, no memory is identifiable at all (Corollary B.1). Under deterministic retrieval, where each query’s sets are the top of one fixed ranking, the sets retrieved for a query at different sizes are nested, and nested sets can leave an invisible change of the same kind as 𝐡∅\mathbf{h}_{\emptyset}, one that raises some memories’ values and lowers the baseline (Lemma B.2). Section 4 removes both obstacles by varying the size and breaking the nesting, and Section 5.3 observes the nesting on real logs.

Private memories per query.

The second convention gives each query bb its own nbn_{b} memories. The TbT_{b} episodes of query bb then retrieve only from these memories, so 𝐗\mathbf{X} splits into one block per query, and the block of query bb has rank at most TbT_{b}.

Proposition 2 (Private memories).

If each query bb has its own nbn_{b} memories and TbT_{b} episodes, at least ∑bmax⁡(nb−Tb, 0)\sum_{b}\max(n_{b}-T_{b},\,0) memories are not identifiable at d=1d=1.

A query asked once determines at most one of its nbn_{b} memory values. Sharing one store across queries lifts this limit, but a fixed retrieval size leaves 𝐡∅\mathbf{h}_{\emptyset} in the log (Theorem 1), so a shared store must be combined with varied retrieval sizes.

Memories always retrieved together.

The third convention follows from ranking by relevance: memories that rank high for exactly the same queries are retrieved in the same episodes, and their columns of 𝐗\mathbf{X} are then identical. At d=1d=1, the invisible change 𝐞{i}−𝐞{j}\mathbf{e}_{\{i\}}-\mathbf{e}_{\{j\}} raises φi\varphi_{i} and lowers φj\varphi_{j} by the same amount, leaving φi+φj\varphi_{i}+\varphi_{j} unchanged; this is aliasing (Rosenbaum and Zubizarreta, 2025). It accounts for the spurious credit that memory systems report for memories co-retrieved with useful ones (Yang et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2026a). Because this change leaves the sum unchanged, Section 4 merges such memories into one.

Retrieval decides what the log can determine.

Theorem 1 and Propositions 1 and 2 identify, from counts alone, which memory values a log leaves undetermined and why. Each undetermined value comes from an invisible change, and each invisible change comes from a retrieval convention (Table 1): a fixed size gives 𝐡B\mathbf{h}_{B}, nested sets give a change like 𝐡∅\mathbf{h}_{\emptyset}, private memories give changes inside each block, and tied memories give 𝐞{i}−𝐞{j}\mathbf{e}_{\{i\}}-\mathbf{e}_{\{j\}}. Every invisible change can be found from the log before any value is estimated, and a change to retrieval can remove it. Memory valuation thus becomes a question of design: which retrievals make the values an agent needs determinable.

4 LEDGER: Valuing Memory Where the Log Allows

Section 3 showed that every undetermined value comes from an invisible change of the log, and that retrieval decides which invisible changes a log contains. This section presents LEDGER, a method built on one object, the invisible changes of the log: every value it reports is one that no invisible change moves, and each of its later actions removes invisible changes (Figure 2). With the log the agent already has, LEDGER first estimates each determined value with a confidence interval and reports every other value as undetermined. It then merges memories that are always retrieved together, which removes the invisible changes between them and keeps every determined value. For the logs the agent will collect, it removes the invisible changes that remain: it varies the retrieval size and fills part of each retrieval with the relevant memories retrieved least often. Appendix C gives the three actions as algorithms.

Estimation.

LEDGER checks the condition of Section 3 numerically (Algorithm 1): with 𝐔\mathbf{U} an orthonormal basis of ker⁡𝐗d\ker\mathbf{X}_{d}, memory ii counts as determined when ‖𝐔⊤​𝐜(i)‖≤τ​‖𝐜(i)‖\|\mathbf{U}^{\!\top}\mathbf{c}^{(i)}\|\leq\tau\,\|\mathbf{c}^{(i)}\|, with τ=10−8\tau=10^{-8}. This check must come first, because a standard solver, such as least squares or ridge regression, returns a number for every memory, including undetermined ones (Lemma A.2). For an undetermined memory, that number estimates only the part of φi\varphi_{i} that no invisible change moves. For each determined memory, LEDGER estimates φi\varphi_{i} from a ridge fit with an interval,

φ^i=(𝐜(i))⊤𝜽^,𝜽^=(𝐗d⊤𝐗d+λ𝐈)−1𝐗d⊤𝐫,φ^i±z1−δ/(2​n)σ^∥𝐗d(𝐗d⊤𝐗d+λ𝐈)−1𝐜(i)∥,\hat{\varphi}_{i}=(\mathbf{c}^{(i)})^{\!\top}\hat{\bm{\theta}},\quad\hat{\bm{\theta}}=(\mathbf{X}_{d}^{\!\top}\mathbf{X}_{d}+\lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{X}_{d}^{\!\top}\mathbf{r},\qquad\hat{\varphi}_{i}\pm z_{1-\delta/(2n)}\,\hat{\sigma}\,\bigl\|\mathbf{X}_{d}(\mathbf{X}_{d}^{\!\top}\mathbf{X}_{d}+\lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{c}^{(i)}\bigr\|, (5)

where λ=10−2\lambda=10^{-2} and σ^\hat{\sigma} is the residual standard deviation. The interval rests on the following:

Proposition 3 (Intervals for determined values).

Suppose the noise εt\varepsilon_{t} has mean zero and is σ\sigma-sub-Gaussian given the retrieved sets, and the retrieved sets do not depend on past outcomes. Then for each determined memory ii, with probability at least 1−δ/n1-\delta/n,

|φ^i−φi|≤σ​2​log⁡(2​n/δ)​‖𝐗d​𝐕−1​𝐜(i)‖+λ​|(𝐜(i))⊤​𝐕−1​𝜽|,𝐕=𝐗d⊤​𝐗d+λ​𝐈,|\hat{\varphi}_{i}-\varphi_{i}|\;\leq\;\sigma\sqrt{2\log(2n/\delta)}\,\bigl\|\mathbf{X}_{d}\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{c}^{(i)}\bigr\|\;+\;\lambda\,\bigl|(\mathbf{c}^{(i)})^{\!\top}\mathbf{V}^{-1}\bm{\theta}\bigr|,\qquad\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{X}_{d}^{\!\top}\mathbf{X}_{d}+\lambda\mathbf{I}, (6)

so the bound holds for all nn memories at once with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta.

The first term is the width of Eq. (5), with the Gaussian quantile z1−δ/(2​n)z_{1-\delta/(2n)} in place of 2​log⁡(2​n/δ)\sqrt{2\log(2n/\delta)}; the second is the ridge bias, which vanishes as λ→0\lambda\to 0 for determined values and does not for undetermined ones (Appendix B.7). The retrieval rule of this section reads the past only through the retrieval counts, so it satisfies the second condition. Every other memory is reported as undetermined, and only determined values guide which memories to keep. Memories that are always retrieved together are among the undetermined ones, and the next action handles them.

Merging.

When memories ii and jj are always retrieved together, the invisible change 𝐞{i}−𝐞{j}\mathbf{e}_{\{i\}}-\mathbf{e}_{\{j\}} raises φi\varphi_{i} and lowers φj\varphi_{j} by the same amount, so the log can determine at most the pair’s total value. LEDGER treats the pair as one memory. It groups memories whose columns of 𝐗\mathbf{X} are identical, which hashing the columns finds in O⁡(n​T)O(nT) time (Algorithm 2), and replaces each group gg by one memory whose column is the shared one and whose value is the sum θ¯g=∑i∈gθ{i}\bar{\theta}_{g}=\sum_{i\in g}\theta_{\{i\}}; this gives a merged matrix 𝐗¯\bar{\mathbf{X}}. Replacing memories changes the parameters, so the question is whether it changes what the log determines. Theorem 2 shows that every determined value is kept.

Theorem 2 (Merging keeps every determined value).

At d=1d=1, range​𝐗1=range​𝐗¯1\mathrm{range}\,\mathbf{X}_{1}=\mathrm{range}\,\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{1}, so the two matrices give the same outcomes. A combination 𝐜⊤​𝛉\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\bm{\theta} is determined by 𝐗1\mathbf{X}_{1} exactly when 𝐜\mathbf{c} takes one value on each group and the corresponding combination of group values is determined by 𝐗¯1\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{1}.

Every value determined before merging is determined after it, and every invisible change between tied memories is gone; the first action then estimates each group value that 𝐗¯1\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{1} determines. The rule reads only retrieval histories: two unrelated memories with the same history are merged, and two near-duplicates retrieved in different episodes stay separate. Merging memories whose histories differ slightly is an approximation. For any grouping at d=1d=1, let a merged memory count as retrieved whenever one of its members is, let DgD_{g} be the largest number of episodes in which group gg was retrieved while one of its members was not, let sg​(𝜽)=∑i∈gθ{i}s_{g}(\bm{\theta})=\sum_{i\in g}\theta_{\{i\}}, and let 𝜽¯=(θ∅,sg1​(𝜽),…,sgm​(𝜽))\bar{\bm{\theta}}=(\theta_{\emptyset},s_{g_{1}}(\bm{\theta}),\dots,s_{g_{m}}(\bm{\theta})).

Theorem 3 (Merging memories with similar histories).

For every combination 𝐜\mathbf{c} in the row space of 𝐗¯1\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{1}, the value that the merged log determines for 𝐜⊤​𝛉¯\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\bar{\bm{\theta}} differs from it by at most

‖𝐜‖σmin+​(𝐗¯1)​∑i=1n|θ{i}|​Dg⁡(i),\frac{\|\mathbf{c}\|}{\sigma^{+}_{\min}(\bar{\mathbf{X}}_{1})}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\theta_{\{i\}}|\,\sqrt{D_{g(i)}}, (7)

where σmin+\sigma^{+}_{\min} is the smallest nonzero singular value and g⁡(i)g(i) is the group of memory ii. The bound is zero when every Dg=0D_{g}=0, which is Theorem 2, and neither its dependence on Dg\sqrt{D_{g}} nor on 1/σmin+1/\sigma^{+}_{\min} can be improved.

Replacing |θ{i}||\theta_{\{i\}}| by the upper end of its interval from Eq. (5) makes the bound computable.

Retrieval.

The next log needs a store shared across queries, at least d+1d+1 distinct retrieval sizes (Proposition 1), and sets that are not nested (Table 1). LEDGER keeps the store shared and draws the size ktk_{t} of each retrieval from at least d+1d+1 values. Let RtR_{t} be the MM memories most similar to qtq_{t}, and let fi​(t)f_{i}(t) be the number of episodes before tt that retrieved memory ii. LEDGER retrieves

St=Lt∪Ht,S_{t}=L_{t}\cup H_{t}, (8)

where LtL_{t} holds the max⁡(1,round⁡(ρ​kt))\max(1,\mathrm{round}(\rho k_{t})) memories of RtR_{t} with the smallest fi​(t)f_{i}(t), and HtH_{t} holds the kt−|Lt|k_{t}-|L_{t}| memories of RtR_{t} most similar to qtq_{t} (Algorithm 3). When LtL_{t} and HtH_{t} overlap, |St|<kt|S_{t}|<k_{t}. The memories in HtH_{t} keep the answer within reach. The memories in LtL_{t} target the least certain estimates: for small λ\lambda, the variance of θ^{i}\hat{\theta}_{\{i\}} is at least σ2/(fi​(t)+λ)\sigma^{2}/(f_{i}(t)+\lambda), since (𝐕−1)i​i≥1/Vi​i(\mathbf{V}^{-1})_{ii}\geq 1/V_{ii} for every positive definite 𝐕\mathbf{V} (Appendix A.5). Because fi​(t)f_{i}(t) changes from pass to pass, one query retrieves different sets over time, which breaks the nesting of top-kk. The baseline test (Definition A.6) checks from the log whether a change like 𝐡∅\mathbf{h}_{\emptyset} remains. We use ρ=0.4\rho=0.4 and M=20M=20. Because this rule changes which memories the reader sees, it trades answer quality for determined values.

5 Experiments

Sections 3 and 4 make four claims that only data can test. First, by Theorem 1 and Proposition 2, the logs of standard benchmarks leave every memory value undetermined; Section 5.2 checks this on fourteen benchmarks. Second, by Proposition 1 and the retrieval rule Eq. (8), LEDGER’s retrieval makes many more values determined; Section 5.3 measures how many, and at what cost in accuracy. Third, by Proposition 3, the interval in Eq. (5) contains each value LEDGER reports at the stated rate. Fourth, by Theorem 2, merging keeps every determined value and makes the total value of each group of tied memories determinable. Section 5.4 tests both.

5.1 Setup

The audit (Section 5.2 and Appendix E) runs fourteen memory benchmarks, each with the retrieval it specifies. The retrieval experiments use three corpora with different structure: HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) and LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2025), whose questions we pool into one shared store per corpus, and LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024), whose questions already share a store within each conversation. Memories are turn- or paragraph-level spans, retrieved by dense similarity over sentence embeddings (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019). Answers come from a hosted reader, gemini-2.5-flash-lite, and are scored by exact match, with the same model as judge otherwise; two further readers, gemini-3.6-flash and gemini-3.7-flash, measure the cost of pooling a store, and they and the use of determined values to decide which memories to keep appear in Appendix F. We compute every identifiability number from 𝐗\mathbf{X} alone, and compare retrieval rules on the same questions, reporting each accuracy difference with a 95%95\% interval and a paired permutation test. Coverage of the intervals is measured on synthetic logs (Appendix D.4). Table 4 names the artifact behind each number below.

5.2 What standard benchmarks determine

For every memory, we checked whether 𝐜(i)\mathbf{c}^{(i)} lies in the row space of 𝐗1\mathbf{X}_{1}, on the logs of fourteen memory benchmarks, each run with the retrieval it specifies and at every kk it uses (Table 2). We ran fourteen benchmarks, each with its own retrieval at every kk it uses, and tested every memory at d=1d=1. Two conventions cause this. Within each block of the log, every episode retrieves the same number of memories (Theorem 1). Most benchmarks also give each question or document its own store, which splits the log into many blocks (Proposition 2). A block is a group of memories never retrieved with a memory outside it, and even a shared store splits into blocks. Block counts follow the order of kk, and “all” retrieves every memory of the context.

All 5555 configurations leave every memory value undetermined, for two reasons. Within each context, every episode retrieves the same number of memories, so a change like 𝐡∅\mathbf{h}_{\emptyset} is invisible in every log (Theorem 1). Twelve of the fourteen benchmarks also give each question, document or conversation its own memories, which splits the log into blocks (Proposition 2). The two benchmarks with one shared store, MultiHopRAG and HELMET, leave every value undetermined because their retrieval size is fixed. LoCoMo shares a store within each conversation and splits its 1,5421{,}542 questions into 1313 blocks at k=5k=5, with the same result. A shared store is therefore necessary and not sufficient. Figure 3a compares LEDGER’s retrieval rule Eq. (8) with deterministic top-kk and with two random rules, ε\varepsilon-greedy and score perturbation, on pooled HotpotQA. The fraction of memories determined is measured on 300300 questions retrieved over 2424 passes (n=2,971n=2{,}971 memories, T=7,200T=7{,}200 episodes), and accuracy on 1,6001{,}600 held-out questions against a pooled store of 15,90015{,}900 memories.

Table 2 tests every memory on 5555 configurations of the 14 benchmarks, at d=1d=1 and therefore at every resolution (Lemma B.3). The first reason is the retrieval size. In every log, all episodes of a context retrieve the same number of memories, kk or the whole context, so the log contains a change like 𝐡∅\mathbf{h}_{\emptyset} that reaches every memory (Theorem 1, and Lemma E.1 when the size differs between contexts). The second reason is the store. Twelve of the fourteen benchmarks give each question, document or conversation its own memories, which splits the log into blocks (Proposition 2). In HotpotQA, for example, each question has about ten memories of its own and is asked once, so varying the size would determine at most one of its ten values. A shared store also splits: MultiHopRAG’s 2,5562{,}556 questions fall into 269269 blocks at k=3k=3 and 1515 at k=10k=10, and HELMET’s 356356 into 4141. A shared store is necessary and not sufficient.

5.3 Retrieval and its cost

Hence, we vary the retrieval size on a shared store. On pooled HotpotQA, four rules draw the size from {3,5,8}\{3,5,8\} (Figure 3a): deterministic top-kk, LEDGER’s rule in Eq. (8), ε\varepsilon greedy and score perturbation. LEDGER’s sets fall below the drawn size in 6.7%6.7\% of episodes, when LtL_{t} and HtH_{t} overlap (Appendix D). The fraction of memories determined is measured on 300300 questions retrieved over 2424 passes (n=2,971n=2{,}971 memories, T=7,200T=7{,}200 episodes). Accuracy is measured on 1,6001{,}600 held-out questions against a pooled store of 15,90015{,}900 memories. The accuracy of the random rules is measured on 300300 questions, with Holm corrected intervals. Deterministic top-kk determines 0.0010.001 of the memories, although its size varies. The reason is nesting: for each question, it retrieves the top of one ranking, so the set at each size contains the smaller ones. In this log, 𝐗𝐰=𝟏T\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{1}_{T} has a least-squares solution with residual 3.1×10−153.1\times 10^{-15}. Lowering the baseline by ss and raising each θ{i}\theta_{\{i\}} by s​wis\,w_{i} then leaves every predicted outcome unchanged, an invisible change (𝐡∅\mathbf{h}_{\emptyset}). Pooling the store has its own cost, which this comparison does not include: on LongMemEval, answering from a pooled store costs 15.715.7 points against each question’s own store (Appendix F.4).

LEDGER’s rule fills part of each set with the relevant memories retrieved least often, and these change from pass to pass, which breaks the nesting. Its residual is 9.2×10−29.2\times 10^{-2}, so 𝟏T\mathbf{1}_{T} lies outside the range of 𝐗\mathbf{X} and this change is gone. The fraction determined rises to 0.7970.797, at a cost of 2.62.6 accuracy points (95%95\% interval [−4.2,−0.9][-4.2,-0.9], permutation p=0.004p=0.004). The random rules trade worse. At about LEDGER’s cost, ε\varepsilon-greedy with ε=0.1\varepsilon=0.1 loses 3.03.0 points and determines 0.0010.001. To determine 0.980.98 or more, the random rules lose at least 13.313.3 points.

LEDGER’s effect on accuracy depends on how much evidence top-kk already finds. We call a memory gold when it holds evidence for the answer. On HotpotQA, LongMemEval and LoCoMo, top-kk retrieves 0.930.93, 0.460.46 and 0.240.24 of the gold memories, and LEDGER changes accuracy by −2.6-2.6, +0.8+0.8 ([−1.9,+3.8][-1.9,+3.8]) and +2.7+2.7 points ([+1.0,+4.4][+1.0,+4.4]). Figure 3b shows the mechanism on HotpotQA. LEDGER replaces some of the similar memories with less-retrieved ones, which can displace gold memories that top-kk had found. On questions where top-kk retrieved every gold memory, LEDGER drops 0.2420.242 of them per question and loses 6.96.9 points. On the other questions, it drops 0.0090.009 and gains 0.70.7. An oracle that applies LEDGER only to the questions where top-kk missed a gold memory removes the cost ([−0.94,+1.44][-0.94,+1.44]). It determines 0.5090.509 of the memories, 64%64\% of LEDGER’s gain.

5.4 Intervals and merging

Checking whether the intervals are valid requires the true values, so we use synthetic logs drawn from the model Eq. (2) with known 𝜽\bm{\theta}, over 3636 settings of nn, kk, TT and λ\lambda at each resolution, with 2020 random designs per setting (Appendix D). A log counts as covered when the interval in Eq. (5), with the noise scale known, contains φi\varphi_{i} for every memory LEDGER reports, and at δ=0.05\delta=0.05 at least 95%95\% of logs should be covered. At d=1d=1, every design has full rank, and at least 97.7%97.7\% of logs are covered in every setting. At d=2d=2, 2424 settings give rank-deficient designs, and at least 99.4%99.4\% of logs are covered in all 3636 settings, in a post hoc analysis (Appendix G.3). Counting every memory instead, coverage falls to 57.2%57.2\% in the worst setting, but every memory there is undetermined. The intervals are 1.521.52 and 1.431.43 times as wide as the pointwise Gaussian interval with the true σ\sigma at d=1d=1 and d=2d=2. The confidence set of Abbasi-Yadkori et al. (2011) is a median 6.66.6 and 3636 times as wide at λ=1\lambda=1, because it bounds every direction of 𝜽\bm{\theta}, while LEDGER bounds only the nn directions 𝐜(i)\mathbf{c}^{(i)} that define the memory values.

Merging replaces tied memories by groups. The value of each tied memory is undetermined, but the total value of its group can be determined, and by Theorem 2 every other memory keeps its status. We therefore count units, meaning memories and groups. On pooled HotpotQA with 100100 questions and LEDGER’s retrieval (n=992n=992 memories, T=2,400T=2{,}400), merging identical histories leaves 869869 units and raises the fraction determined from 0.8150.815 to 0.9920.992. Merging also helps on conversational memory. On two LoCoMo conversations (n=788n=788 memories), the standard log determines no value (Table 2). Three passes of retrieval with score perturbation determine 79.0%79.0\% of their memories, and merging raises this to 95.7%95.7\% of the units.

6 Conclusion

A retrieval log determines a memory’s value only if the retrievals separate that memory from the others, and this can be checked from the log before any outcome is seen. Standard benchmarks fail this check: a fixed retrieval size and private stores leave every memory value undetermined in all 5555 configurations of fourteen benchmarks. Both causes are choices about retrieval, so changing retrieval removes them. LEDGER raises the fraction of memories determined from 0.0010.001 to 0.7970.797 at a cost of 2.62.6 accuracy points. Every value LEDGER reports is determined by the log and comes with a confidence interval, and every other value is reported as undetermined. Memory benchmarks should report which values their logs determine alongside accuracy. Finding at query time the questions where spreading retrieval costs nothing is the open problem that remains.

AI use statement

Generative AI tools helped design experiments and choose their parameters, generate synthetic data, write code, and clean datasets. On the literature, they helped search, summarize, and analyze prior work and format references. On the paper, they helped create figures and tables, draft text, and edit it. We reviewed all AI-assisted work and checked it in four ways. Every empirical claim was pre-registered with a decision rule, and three claims that failed their rule were withdrawn (Appendix G). Every reported number is reproduced from committed artifacts and was reconciled against them in a separate audit. Every theoretical claim was tested on synthetic designs with known ground truth. Every bibliography entry was verified against its source. We take full responsibility for the content of this paper.

Ethics statement

This work involves no human subjects, no new data collection, and no release of new data, so no IRB review was required. All experiments use public benchmarks under their published licenses; their contents are encyclopedic text and synthetically generated dialogue, and we neither collected nor inferred personal information from them. Two consequences of the method deserve explicit statement. First, the instrumentation we recommend is not free to the end user: an AA-optimal tie-break deliberately selects among answer-preserving retrieval sets by information gain, and we measure an accuracy cost whose sign depends on the corpus, so a practitioner adopting it trades some answer quality for the ability to value memory at all. We report both signs, the mechanism that produces them (Section 4), and a restriction that removes the cost on the corpus where it is largest, so that this trade is made deliberately and not inherited from a default. Second, a framework that makes the value of an individual stored memory identifiable thereby makes attribution to that memory identifiable. The same quantity that justifies retaining or deleting a record supports profiling the interactions the record was derived from. We declare no conflicts of interest. On research integrity, claims here are pre-registered, null and negative results are reported alongside positive ones (Appendix F), and corrections to values that appeared in earlier drafts are recorded in the paper.

Reproducibility statement

The two modeling assumptions are stated in Section 2 and their scope is discussed in Appendix A.3; every theoretical claim in Sections 3 to 4 is proved in full in Appendix B, with the merge-map construction and its complexity given as explicit algorithms in Appendix C; the synthetic generator used to check those claims against known ground truth is specified in Appendix D, and the tables reporting every headline number are generated from committed artifacts and collected in Appendix F. Anonymous source code, the dated pre-registration documents, the exact benchmark preparation and store-construction steps, and the artifacts from which every table is generated are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ledger-review-AF71/. The theoretical track (identifiability verdicts, ranks, the exact quotient, and all synthetic experiments) is fully reproducible and deterministic from the released code and a fixed seed, since it consults no model. The empirical track is reproducible in its design and not claimed to be bit-reproducible in its outcomes: the retrieval logs, design matrices and identifiability measurements regenerate byte-identically from the released inputs, while the reader accuracies depend on hosted model inference that we cannot pin, so we report paired comparisons with intervals and the sample sizes they were computed at. Appendix G documents the defects we found in our own pipeline, the values they affected, and the corrected values, so that a reader attempting to reproduce this work knows which numbers changed and why.

Appendix

Appendix A Preliminaries and Related Work

This appendix collects the classical results the paper builds on and fixes the quantities it reports. Appendix A.1 states when a linear model determines a linear functional, Appendix A.2 writes memory values as such functionals, and Appendix A.3 discusses the scope of the two assumptions. Appendix A.4 applies these results to a retrieval log, Appendix A.5 gives the optimal-design and confidence-set results that Sections 4 and 5 use, and Appendix A.6 relates the work to the literature. Notation and terms are collected in Appendix I.

A.1 Linear models and estimability

Consider the linear model 𝐫=𝐀​𝜷+𝜺\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{A}\bm{\beta}+\bm{\varepsilon} with a known matrix 𝐀∈ℝT×p\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times p}, an unknown parameter 𝜷∈ℝp\bm{\beta}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} and 𝔼​𝜺=𝟎\mathbb{E}\,\bm{\varepsilon}=\mathbf{0}. The question is which linear functionals 𝐜⊤​𝜷\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\bm{\beta} the data determine.

Definition A.1 (Estimable functional).

A linear functional 𝐜⊤​𝜷\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\bm{\beta} is estimable if some 𝐚∈ℝT\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{T} satisfies 𝔼⁡[𝐚⊤​𝐫]=𝐜⊤​𝜷\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{a}^{\!\top}\mathbf{r}]=\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\bm{\beta} for every 𝜷∈ℝp\bm{\beta}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}.

Lemma A.1 (Rao, 1973, Section 4a.2).

𝐜⊤​𝜷\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\bm{\beta} is estimable if and only if 𝐜∈range​𝐀⊤\mathbf{c}\in\mathrm{range}\,\mathbf{A}^{\!\top}, equivalently 𝐜⊤​𝐡=0\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\mathbf{h}=0 for every 𝐡∈ker⁡𝐀\mathbf{h}\in\ker\mathbf{A}. If it is estimable, 𝐜⊤​𝛃^\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\hat{\bm{\beta}} takes the same value for every least-squares solution 𝛃^\hat{\bm{\beta}}, and when Cov​𝛆=σ2​𝐈\mathrm{Cov}\,\bm{\varepsilon}=\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I} this value is the best linear unbiased estimator of 𝐜⊤​𝛃\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\bm{\beta}.

The first statement follows in one line: 𝔼⁡[𝐚⊤​𝐫]=(𝐀⊤​𝐚)⊤​𝜷\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{a}^{\!\top}\mathbf{r}]=(\mathbf{A}^{\!\top}\mathbf{a})^{\!\top}\bm{\beta} equals 𝐜⊤​𝜷\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\bm{\beta} for every 𝜷\bm{\beta} exactly when 𝐀⊤​𝐚=𝐜\mathbf{A}^{\!\top}\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{c}. The equivalence with the kernel condition is range​𝐀⊤=(ker⁡𝐀)⟂\mathrm{range}\,\mathbf{A}^{\!\top}=(\ker\mathbf{A})^{\perp}. Two further facts are used throughout. First, ker⁡𝐀=ker⁡(𝐀⊤​𝐀)\ker\mathbf{A}=\ker(\mathbf{A}^{\!\top}\mathbf{A}): if 𝐀⊤​𝐀𝐡=𝟎\mathbf{A}^{\!\top}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{h}=\mathbf{0}, then ‖𝐀𝐡‖2=𝐡⊤​𝐀⊤​𝐀𝐡=0\|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{h}\|^{2}=\mathbf{h}^{\!\top}\mathbf{A}^{\!\top}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{h}=0, and the converse is immediate. Estimability is therefore decided by the Gram matrix 𝐀⊤​𝐀\mathbf{A}^{\!\top}\mathbf{A} alone. Second, a vector 𝐡∈ker⁡𝐀\mathbf{h}\in\ker\mathbf{A} is invisible in the data: 𝜷\bm{\beta} and 𝜷+s​𝐡\bm{\beta}+s\mathbf{h} give the same distribution of 𝐫\mathbf{r} for every s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}, while 𝐜⊤​𝜷\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\bm{\beta} changes by s​𝐜⊤​𝐡s\,\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\mathbf{h}. The next lemma states what a solver reports for a functional that is not estimable.

Lemma A.2 (What a solver reports).

Write 𝐜=𝐜1+𝐜2\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{c}_{1}+\mathbf{c}_{2} with 𝐜1∈range​𝐀⊤\mathbf{c}_{1}\in\mathrm{range}\,\mathbf{A}^{\!\top} and 𝐜2∈ker⁡𝐀\mathbf{c}_{2}\in\ker\mathbf{A}. The least-squares solutions are 𝐀†​𝐫+ker⁡𝐀\mathbf{A}^{\dagger}\mathbf{r}+\ker\mathbf{A}, where 𝐀†\mathbf{A}^{\dagger} is the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse. If 𝐜2≠𝟎\mathbf{c}_{2}\neq\mathbf{0}, then 𝐜⊤​𝛃^\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\hat{\bm{\beta}} takes every real value as 𝛃^\hat{\bm{\beta}} ranges over these solutions. The minimum-norm solution and the ridge solution (𝐀⊤​𝐀+λ​𝐈)−1​𝐀⊤​𝐫(\mathbf{A}^{\!\top}\mathbf{A}+\lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{A}^{\!\top}\mathbf{r}, for every λ>0\lambda>0, lie in range​𝐀⊤\mathrm{range}\,\mathbf{A}^{\!\top}, so each reports 𝐜1⊤​𝛃^\mathbf{c}_{1}^{\!\top}\hat{\bm{\beta}}: an estimate of 𝐜1⊤​𝛃\mathbf{c}_{1}^{\!\top}\bm{\beta}, which differs from 𝐜⊤​𝛃\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\bm{\beta} by 𝐜2⊤​𝛃\mathbf{c}_{2}^{\!\top}\bm{\beta}.

Proof.

If 𝜷^\hat{\bm{\beta}} is a least-squares solution, so is 𝜷^+s​𝐜2\hat{\bm{\beta}}+s\mathbf{c}_{2} for every ss, and 𝐜⊤​(𝜷^+s​𝐜2)=𝐜⊤​𝜷^+s​‖𝐜2‖2\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}(\hat{\bm{\beta}}+s\mathbf{c}_{2})=\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\hat{\bm{\beta}}+s\|\mathbf{c}_{2}\|^{2} takes every real value. The minimum-norm solution 𝐀†​𝐫\mathbf{A}^{\dagger}\mathbf{r} lies in range​𝐀⊤\mathrm{range}\,\mathbf{A}^{\!\top} by definition of the pseudoinverse, and the ridge solution equals 𝐀⊤​(𝐀𝐀⊤+λ​𝐈)−1​𝐫\mathbf{A}^{\!\top}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{\!\top}+\lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{r}, which lies there as well. For any 𝜷^∈range​𝐀⊤\hat{\bm{\beta}}\in\mathrm{range}\,\mathbf{A}^{\!\top}, 𝐜2⊤​𝜷^=0\mathbf{c}_{2}^{\!\top}\hat{\bm{\beta}}=0. ∎

The reported number and its standard error look the same whether or not 𝐜2=𝟎\mathbf{c}_{2}=\mathbf{0}, so nothing in the output shows that the part 𝐜2⊤​𝜷\mathbf{c}_{2}^{\!\top}\bm{\beta} was set to zero by the solver. LEDGER therefore tests 𝐜2=𝟎\mathbf{c}_{2}=\mathbf{0} before it estimates (Section 4).

Lemma A.3 (Appending a column).

For 𝐀∈ℝT×p\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times p} and 𝐚∈ℝT\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{T}, rank[𝐚∣𝐀]=rank𝐀+𝟏[𝐚∉range𝐀]\mathrm{rank}\,[\mathbf{a}\mid\mathbf{A}]=\mathrm{rank}\,\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{1}[\mathbf{a}\notin\mathrm{range}\,\mathbf{A}]. Appending columns to 𝐀\mathbf{A} never makes a functional of the original parameters estimable that was not estimable before.

Proof.

The first statement is the definition of rank. For the second, let 𝐡∈ker⁡𝐀\mathbf{h}\in\ker\mathbf{A} with 𝐜⊤​𝐡≠0\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\mathbf{h}\neq 0. Then (𝐡,𝟎)∈ker⁡[𝐀∣𝐁](\mathbf{h},\mathbf{0})\in\ker[\mathbf{A}\mid\mathbf{B}] for any appended block 𝐁\mathbf{B}, and its inner product with (𝐜,𝟎)(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{0}) is 𝐜⊤​𝐡≠0\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\mathbf{h}\neq 0, so (𝐜,𝟎)(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{0}) is not estimable by Lemma A.1. ∎

A.2 Set functions, dividends and values

The results of Appendix A.1 apply to memory values once each value is a linear functional of a parameter vector. Möbius dividends provide that vector.

Definition A.2 (Möbius dividends; Harsanyi, 1963; Grabisch et al., 2000).

For v:2[n]→ℝv:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb{R}, the Möbius dividend of B⊆[n]B\subseteq[n] is θB=∑A⊆B(−1)|B∖A|​v​(A)\theta_{B}=\sum_{A\subseteq B}(-1)^{|B\setminus A|}\,v(A). Then v⁡(S)=∑B⊆SθBv(S)=\sum_{B\subseteq S}\theta_{B} for every S⊆[n]S\subseteq[n], and the dividends are the unique numbers with this property. We call vv dd-additive if θB=0\theta_{B}=0 whenever |B|>d|B|>d.

The dividend θB\theta_{B} is the part of vv that the members of BB create jointly and no proper subset of BB creates. The dividend of the empty set is θ∅=v⁡(∅)\theta_{\emptyset}=v(\emptyset), the baseline. The Shapley value (Shapley, 1953) of element ii is

φi​(v)=∑S⊆[n]∖{i}|S|!​(n−|S|−1)!n!​[v⁡(S∪{i})−v⁡(S)],\varphi_{i}(v)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]\setminus\{i\}}\frac{|S|!\,(n-|S|-1)!}{n!}\bigl[v(S\cup\{i\})-v(S)\bigr],

the average marginal contribution of ii over all orders in which the elements can be added.

Lemma A.4 (Harsanyi, 1963).

φi=∑B∋iθB/|B|\varphi_{i}=\sum_{B\ni i}\theta_{B}/|B|. If vv is dd-additive, then φi=(𝐜(i))⊤​𝛉\varphi_{i}=(\mathbf{c}^{(i)})^{\!\top}\bm{\theta}, where 𝛉=(θB)|B|≤d\bm{\theta}=(\theta_{B})_{|B|\leq d} and cB(i)=𝟏[i∈B]/|B|c^{(i)}_{B}=\mathbf{1}[i\in B]/|B|. The baseline θ∅\theta_{\emptyset} does not enter φi\varphi_{i}.

Each dividend is thus shared equally among its members. Other values are linear in the dividends with other coefficients. The Banzhaf value (Banzhaf III, 1964), which averages the marginal contribution of ii over all subsets with equal weight, is ∑B∋i21−|B|​θB\sum_{B\ni i}2^{1-|B|}\theta_{B}. More generally, every probabilistic value (Weber, 1988) averages the marginal contributions v⁡(S∪{i})−v⁡(S)=∑A⊆SθA∪{i}v(S\cup\{i\})-v(S)=\sum_{A\subseteq S}\theta_{A\cup\{i\}} with some weights, so it is linear in 𝜽\bm{\theta}, and the estimability test of Appendix A.1 applies to it with its own coefficient vector. At d=1d=1 every marginal contribution equals θ{i}\theta_{\{i\}}, so every probabilistic value of ii, the Shapley value included, equals θ{i}\theta_{\{i\}}.

A.3 Assumptions and their scope

Section 2 states two assumptions. This subsection says what each requires, what is lost when it fails, and the further condition that estimation needs.

Assumption 1.

The assumption restricts neither the language model, the encoder nor the query distribution. It states that the expected outcome of an episode is a function of the query and the retrieved set, which is what it means for retrieval to matter, and that the deviations from this function are conditionally sub-Gaussian, which holds for every bounded outcome. The outcome may be binary or graded. Decisions about the whole store, such as what to keep and what to merge, need the query-averaged value

v⁡(S)=𝔼q∼𝒟Q​[vq​(S)],v(S)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D}_{Q}}\bigl[v_{q}(S)\bigr], (9)

and the paper values memories under this vv.

Assumption 2.

The Shapley value is defined for every vv, and Lemma A.4 writes it in dividends of every order. The resolution dd keeps the dividends of order at most dd, and the next proposition gives exactly what the others contribute.

Proposition A.1 (Truncation error).

For any vv and any dd, let v(d)​(S)=∑B⊆S,|B|≤dθBv^{(d)}(S)=\sum_{B\subseteq S,\,|B|\leq d}\theta_{B}. Then

φi​(v)−φi​(v(d))=∑B∋i,|B|>dθB|B|,so|φi​(v)−φi​(v(d))|≤1d+1​∑B∋i,|B|>d|θB|.\varphi_{i}(v)-\varphi_{i}\bigl(v^{(d)}\bigr)\;=\;\sum_{B\ni i,\;|B|>d}\frac{\theta_{B}}{|B|},\qquad\text{so}\qquad\bigl|\varphi_{i}(v)-\varphi_{i}(v^{(d)})\bigr|\leq\frac{1}{d+1}\sum_{B\ni i,\,|B|>d}|\theta_{B}|. (10)
Proof.

The dividends of v(d)v^{(d)} are those of vv of order at most dd and zero otherwise, by uniqueness in Definition A.2. Subtracting the two expressions of Lemma A.4 gives the identity, and |B|≥d+1|B|\geq d+1 gives the bound. ∎

The proposition needs no assumption on vv. When Assumption 2 fails, the omitted dividends also enter the noise εt\varepsilon_{t}, and the estimates at resolution dd are biased wherever these dividends correlate with the design. A memory undetermined at resolution dd remains undetermined at every higher resolution (Appendix H.1), so the negative results of Section 5 hold whatever the true order of vv.

Exogeneity.

Write vq=v+δqv_{q}=v+\delta_{q}, so that 𝔼q​δq​(S)=0\mathbb{E}_{q}\,\delta_{q}(S)=0 for every SS. The noise of Eq. (2) is then εt=ηt+δqt​(St)\varepsilon_{t}=\eta_{t}+\delta_{q_{t}}(S_{t}). Retrieval reads qtq_{t} when it chooses StS_{t}, so δqt​(St)\delta_{q_{t}}(S_{t}) can correlate with the design.

Definition A.3 (Exogeneity).

A log is exogenous at resolution dd if 𝔼⁡[𝐗d⊤​𝜹]=𝟎\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathbf{X}_{d}^{\!\top}\bm{\delta}\bigr]=\mathbf{0}, where 𝜹t=δqt​(St)\bm{\delta}_{t}=\delta_{q_{t}}(S_{t}).

A log is exogenous, for example, when StS_{t} is independent of qtq_{t}: then 𝔼[𝟏[B⊆St]δqt(St)]=𝔼St[𝟏[B⊆St]𝔼qδq(St)]=0\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}[B\subseteq S_{t}]\,\delta_{q_{t}}(S_{t})]=\mathbb{E}_{S_{t}}\bigl[\mathbf{1}[B\subseteq S_{t}]\,\mathbb{E}_{q}\,\delta_{q}(S_{t})\bigr]=0. Retrieval by relevance makes StS_{t} depend on qtq_{t}, so the logs of Section 5 need not be exogenous, and the values LEDGER reports on them describe the association between retrieval and outcome in the log. Identifiability involves 𝐗d\mathbf{X}_{d} alone, so it is unaffected; only estimation is. Appending query features ψ⁡(qt)\psi(q_{t}) as columns of the design removes the part of 𝜹\bm{\delta} in their span, and by Lemma A.3 every result on identifiability in Section 3 holds for the augmented design. Estimation needs one further condition, on adaptivity: Proposition 3 requires that the retrieved sets do not depend on past outcomes. LEDGER’s rule Eq. (8) depends on the past only through 𝐗\mathbf{X}, so it satisfies this condition.

The linear model.

Under Assumptions 1 and 2, rt=v⁡(St)+εtr_{t}=v(S_{t})+\varepsilon_{t} with vv dd-additive. By Definition A.2,

The paper uses the following definition throughout.

Definition A.4 (Determined value, fraction determined).

At resolution dd, memory ii is identifiable, and its value is determined, if φi\varphi_{i} is estimable in 𝐫=𝐗d​𝜽+𝜺\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{X}_{d}\bm{\theta}+\bm{\varepsilon}, that is, if 𝐜(i)∈range​𝐗d⊤\mathbf{c}^{(i)}\in\mathrm{range}\,\mathbf{X}_{d}^{\!\top}. Otherwise its value is undetermined. The fraction determined is the number of identifiable memories divided by nn; after merging, it is the number of determined units divided by the number of units.

At d=1d=1, 𝐜(i)=(0,𝐞i)\mathbf{c}^{(i)}=(0,\mathbf{e}_{i}), so memory ii is identifiable exactly when (0,𝐞i)(0,\mathbf{e}_{i}) is orthogonal to ker⁡𝐗1\ker\mathbf{X}_{1}. Unless stated otherwise, every fraction in the paper is computed at d=1d=1 with the baseline column included.

Blocks.

The co-retrieval graph has one vertex per memory and an edge between mim_{i} and mjm_{j} whenever co⁡(mi,mj)>0\mathrm{co}(m_{i},m_{j})>0.

Definition A.5 (Blocks).

The blocks of a log are the connected components of the co-retrieval graph restricted to the memories retrieved at least once. Block bb contains nbn_{b} memories and the TbT_{b} episodes whose retrieved sets lie in it.

The members of one retrieved set are pairwise adjacent, so every episode belongs to exactly one block.

Lemma A.5 (Block rank).

After permuting rows and columns, the columns of 𝐗\mathbf{X} for the retrieved memories form a block-diagonal matrix with diagonal blocks 𝐗(b)∈{0,1}Tb×nb\mathbf{X}^{(b)}\in\{0,1\}^{T_{b}\times n_{b}}, and the columns for memories never retrieved are zero. Hence rank​𝐗=∑brank​𝐗(b)≤∑bmin⁡(Tb,nb)\mathrm{rank}\,\mathbf{X}=\sum_{b}\mathrm{rank}\,\mathbf{X}^{(b)}\leq\sum_{b}\min(T_{b},n_{b}).

The baseline column 𝟏T\mathbf{1}_{T} meets every block, so 𝐗1\mathbf{X}_{1} is not block-diagonal, and rank​𝐗1≤rank​𝐗+1\mathrm{rank}\,\mathbf{X}_{1}\leq\mathrm{rank}\,\mathbf{X}+1 by Lemma A.3. A memory that is never retrieved has a zero column, so 𝐞i\mathbf{e}_{i} lies in ker⁡𝐗1\ker\mathbf{X}_{1} and its value is undetermined.

Tied memories.

If memories ii and jj are retrieved in exactly the same episodes, their columns of 𝐗\mathbf{X} are equal, and 𝐞{i}−𝐞{j}∈ker⁡𝐗1\mathbf{e}_{\{i\}}-\mathbf{e}_{\{j\}}\in\ker\mathbf{X}_{1}. Its inner product with 𝐜(i)\mathbf{c}^{(i)} is 11, so neither value is determined, while the sum θ{i}+θ{j}\theta_{\{i\}}+\theta_{\{j\}} is orthogonal to this change. Merging (Section 4) replaces each such group by one unit valued by this sum.

A.5 Optimal design and confidence sets

The variance of an estimate.

With 𝐕=𝐗d⊤​𝐗d+λ​𝐈\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{X}_{d}^{\!\top}\mathbf{X}_{d}+\lambda\mathbf{I} and noise covariance σ2​𝐈\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I}, the ridge estimate of Eq. (5) satisfies

Var⁡(𝐜⊤​𝜽^)=σ2​𝐜⊤​𝐕−1​𝐗d⊤​𝐗d​𝐕−1​𝐜=σ2​(𝐜⊤​𝐕−1​𝐜−λ​‖𝐕−1​𝐜‖2),\mathrm{Var}\bigl(\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\hat{\bm{\theta}}\bigr)=\sigma^{2}\,\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}_{d}^{\!\top}\mathbf{X}_{d}\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{c}=\sigma^{2}\bigl(\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{c}-\lambda\,\|\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{c}\|^{2}\bigr),

The first term dominates for small λ\lambda, so tr⁡(𝐕−1)\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{V}^{-1}) is, up to σ2\sigma^{2}, the total variance of the coordinate estimates. shows that adding an episode with row 𝐱\mathbf{x} reduces tr⁡(𝐕−1)\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{V}^{-1}) by ‖𝐕−1​𝐱‖2/(1+𝐱⊤​𝐕−1​𝐱)\|\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{x}\|^{2}/(1+\mathbf{x}^{\!\top}\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{x}), and updates 𝐕−1\mathbf{V}^{-1} in O⁡(pd2)O(p_{d}^{2}) time.

The bound behind LEDGER’s retrieval rule.

For every positive definite 𝐕\mathbf{V} and every ii,

(𝐕−1)i​i≥1Vi​i,(\mathbf{V}^{-1})_{ii}\;\geq\;\frac{1}{V_{ii}},

A.6 Related work

This work meets six lines of research: memory management by proxy statistics, memory value learned from outcomes, cooperative-game attribution, budgeted selection, graph-structured retrieval, and the classical theory of estimation and design. Each has produced strong systems, and this paper adopts much of their machinery. It asks a question none of them poses: which memory values a retrieval log determines.

Memory management by proxy.

Persistent memory is a primary determinant of long-horizon agent performance (Pink et al., 2025; Du et al., 2025), and a body of work decides what to retain. FadeMem (Wei et al., 2026a) applies differential decay across a two-layer hierarchy, modulating an exponential forgetting rate by semantic relevance, access frequency and recency. Budget-curated forgetting (Wu et al., 2026a) formulates retention as bounded optimisation over similar statistics, and ACT-R-inspired architectures (Honda et al., 2025) import the activation equation of a model of human memory. SSGM (Lam et al., 2026) decouples memory evolution from execution with consistency checks, temporal decay and access control, and Aeon (Arslan, 2026) targets the throughput of the same operations. These systems differ in the statistic they use and share its status: it is a function of content and access, fixed before any outcome is observed, and validated by downstream accuracy. Two memories with the same content and access pattern therefore receive the same score whatever they contribute. Access frequency is the diagonal of 𝐗⊤​𝐗\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}\mathbf{X} in Eq. (1), so these statistics record how often a memory is used, which decides whether its contribution can be learned and does not measure it (Appendix H.3).

Memory value learned from outcomes.

A second line learns a value signal from downstream reward. RMM (Tan et al., 2025) refines retrieval online by reinforcement learning from the evidence the model cites. MemRL (Zhang et al., 2026) applies reinforcement learning to episodic memory updates, with a two-phase retrieval that filters for high-utility entries. AttriMem (Li et al., 2026) uses token-level attribution to the final answer as a local reward for a memory-construction policy, and Memory-R1 (Yan et al., 2026b) and Memory-R2 (Yan et al., 2026a) train memory operations from outcome rewards, the latter with explicit credit assignment over operations. RoMeRL (Yang et al., 2026) names the memory-reward trap: irrelevant memories accrue positive credit because they are retrieved together with useful ones. These methods learn a signal and show that it helps; none characterises when the signal is recoverable. The memory-reward trap is the invisible change 𝐞{i}−𝐞{j}\mathbf{e}_{\{i\}}-\mathbf{e}_{\{j\}} of tied memories (Section 3): when two memories share a retrieval history, no procedure that reads the log can separate their credit, and the answer consistent with the data is to report the pair as undetermined and merge it. When every rollout retrieves the same number of memories, the credit of every memory is undetermined (Theorem 1). Both statements constrain every method in this line, LEDGER included.

Cooperative-game attribution.

The Shapley value (Shapley, 1953) is the canonical answer to what a participant contributes to a joint outcome, and Data Shapley (Ghorbani and Zou, 2019) brought it to machine learning. It has since been applied to retrieved content. Ye and Yoganarasimhan (2025) value source documents in summaries with a clustering approximation and accuracy bounds. MaxShapley (Patel et al., 2025) obtains exact values in polynomial time from a decomposable max-sum utility. Shapley context pruning (Chen et al., 2026b) and RepoShapley (Huo et al., 2026) apply the same machinery to passage reranking and to repository-level code context, and MemLens (Wei et al., 2026b) defines a Memory Shapley value and uses it to drive retention. General estimators approximate interactions of any order by sampling coalitions (Tsai et al., 2023; Fumagalli et al., 2023; Kang et al., 2025), and context attribution fits a surrogate to random ablations of the prompt (Cohen-Wang et al., 2024). We adopt the same notion of value. The difference is access. Each method above evaluates v⁡(S)v(S) on coalitions of its choosing, which requires replaying the system on subsets that never occurred. A deployed agent has only the coalitions that did occur, and LEDGER asks which values those determine. Because the Shapley value is a fixed linear functional of the Möbius dividends (Harsanyi, 1963; Grabisch et al., 2000) (Lemma A.4), the answer is exact and requires no sampling, and the error of truncating to resolution dd is written in closed form (Proposition A.1).

Budgeted selection.

Retention under a budget is a selection problem, and submodular maximisation supplies its standard guarantees (Nemhauser et al., 1978; Conforti and Cornuéjols, 1984; Buchbinder et al., 2014). PACMS (Ghulyani et al., 2026) applies a facility-location objective with lazy greedy selection to pooled memory entries, turns and tool outputs. These guarantees hold for a proxy objective defined in embedding space, and coverage in that space is assumed to track usefulness. LEDGER’s retention objective (Appendix F) is the estimated value itself. We do not assume that it is submodular, and we claim no guarantee that would require it.

Graph-structured retrieval and coarsening.

Retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020) conditions generation on a retrieved set, and graphs structure what is retrieved. HippoRAG (Jiménez Gutiérrez et al., 2024) combines a knowledge graph with Personalized PageRank, G-Retriever (He et al., 2024) retrieves subgraphs as a prize-collecting Steiner tree, and RAGraph (Jiang et al., 2024) provides a general framework for retrieval-augmented graph learning. For multi-hop reasoning, RoG (Luo et al., 2024) generates relation paths as plans, ToG-2 (Ma et al., 2025) alternates knowledge-guided and context-enhanced retrieval, StructRAG (Li et al., 2025) structures information at inference time, and HopRAG (Liu et al., 2025) traverses passages with logic-aware hops. GAM (Wu et al., 2026b) and TierMem (Zhu et al., 2026) organise agent memory hierarchically. The graphs in these systems encode relations between contents. The graph in this paper encodes usage: an edge joins two memories retrieved in the same episode, and by Eq. (1) its weighted adjacency matrix is the Gram matrix of the valuation problem. Merging is likewise distinct from graph coarsening (Joly and Keriven, 2024; Han et al., 2024), whose guarantees state that a coarsened graph approximates the original within a constant. Merging memories with identical retrieval histories keeps every determined value exactly (Theorem 2), because the only quantities it removes are the splits of each group’s total, which the log never determined.

Estimation, design and bandits.

Estimability of linear functionals under a rank-deficient design is classical (Rao, 1973), and so is the aliasing of effects that never vary apart (Rosenbaum and Zubizarreta, 2025). Our contribution here is the identity Eq. (1): the design matrix of memory valuation is determined by counts that memory systems already record, so these results apply to them. LEDGER’s intervals are per-functional; the self-normalised confidence set of Abbasi-Yadkori et al. (2011) bounds every direction at once and remains valid under adaptive designs, at a width we compare in Section 5.4. Because only a set-level outcome is observed, the setting has the full-bandit feedback of combinatorial and top-kk bandits (Chen et al., 2013; Rejwan and Mansour, 2020), and this is why the design, and not the reward model, limits what can be learned. LEDGER’s retrieval rule is motivated by optimal design (Pukelsheim, 2006), with one constraint that classical design does not have: it may choose only among memories relevant to the query, which is the source of the accuracy cost measured in Section 5.3.

Slate evaluation and intervention harvesting.

Two neighbours are close enough to state the difference precisely. Slate off-policy evaluation (Swaminathan et al., 2017) builds the same Gram matrix from logged set-valued actions. Its estimand is the value of a policy, for which the kernel can be projected out; ours is the value of each memory, and the kernel decides which of those the log determines. Recent work there reduces variance by learning an abstraction of the slate space (Kiyohara et al., 2024), which resembles merging; merging is forced by Theorem 2 and is exact. Intervention harvesting (Agarwal et al., 2019) recovers position bias from variation that occurs naturally across deployed rankers. LEDGER addresses the complementary case, in which that variation does not occur, and measures what it costs to create it (Section 5.3).

Evaluation protocols.

Benchmarks for long-horizon memory and multi-hop retrieval, including LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024), LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2025) and HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018), measure answer accuracy under a fixed retrieval protocol, and they measure it well. Their protocols give each question its own memories or retrieve a fixed number of items, and under either protocol the log determines no memory value (Section 5.2). Appendix E lists the fourteen benchmarks we audit and the protocol of each.

Under deterministic top-kk, each query qq has a fixed ranking of the memories, and every set retrieved for qq is a prefix of it. Let k1k_{1} be the smallest retrieval size, let AqA_{q} be the k1k_{1} memories ranked highest for qq, and let C=⋃qAqC=\bigcup_{q}A_{q}.

The hypothesis holds whenever the queries have private stores, and in a shared store it holds when no set retrieved for one query contains a memory ranked in the top k1k_{1} for another. The baseline test (Definition A.6) detects the resulting change whether or not the hypothesis holds exactly: under deterministic top-kk on pooled HotpotQA its residual is 3.1×10−153.1\times 10^{-15}, zero up to rounding (Section 5.3).
