Appendix C Algorithms

This appendix gives LEDGER’s three actions as algorithms, in the order of Section 4: the test and the estimates (Algorithm 1), merging (Algorithm 2) and retrieval (Algorithm 3), followed by the baseline test and the cost of each step. The released code implements them as stated; its names for the parameters are given where they differ from the paper’s.

C.1 The test and the estimates

Algorithm 1 decides, for each memory, whether the log determines its value, and estimates only the values it determines. The test comes first, because the ridge solution returns a number for every memory (Lemma A.2). It uses the kernel of the Gram matrix, which equals ker⁡𝐗d\ker\mathbf{X}_{d} (Appendix A.1) and has pdp_{d} rows whatever TT is.

In all experiments, λ=10−2\lambda=10^{-2}, τ=10−8\tau=10^{-8} and δ=0.05\delta=0.05. The basis 𝐔\mathbf{U} keeps the eigenvectors of 𝐌\mathbf{M} with eigenvalue at most pd​ϵmach​max⁡(λmax​(𝐌),1)p_{d}\,\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}\max(\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{M}),1), and σ^\hat{\sigma} uses the effective degrees of freedom tr⁡(𝐕−1​𝐌)\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{M}). For pd>4,000p_{d}>4{,}000, the test solves one least squares problem per memory by LSMR instead of forming 𝐔\mathbf{U}. The width uses ‖𝐗d​𝐕−1​𝐜‖2=𝐜⊤​𝐕−1​𝐌𝐕−1​𝐜\|\mathbf{X}_{d}\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{c}\|^{2}=\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{c}, so it needs 𝐌\mathbf{M} and not 𝐗d\mathbf{X}_{d}. At d=1d=1, 𝐜(i)=(0,𝐞i)\mathbf{c}^{(i)}=(0,\mathbf{e}_{i}), so the test reads the ii-th row of 𝐔\mathbf{U} and the estimate is θ^{i}\hat{\theta}_{\{i\}}.

C.2 Merging

Algorithm 2 groups memories with identical columns of 𝐗\mathbf{X} and builds the merged matrix of Theorem 2. Hashing makes it linear in the size of the log.

The memories never retrieved share the empty history and form one group with a zero column, which stays undetermined. LEDGER then applies Algorithm 1 to 𝐗¯\bar{\mathbf{X}}, with one unit per group; by Theorem 2, every value determined before merging is determined after it.

Merging similar histories.

Theorem 3 bounds the error of merging memories whose histories differ. Theorem 3 bounds the error of merging memories whose histories differ. LEDGER finds candidate pairs of units by locality-sensitive hashing of their columns and keeps those whose columns differ in at most δmax=8\delta_{\max}=8 episodes. It accepts a candidate unconditionally when the merged unit’s total is undetermined before the merge and determined after it, and otherwise when the bound Eq. (7), with each |θ{i}||\theta_{\{i\}}| replaced by |θ^{i}|+1.96​sei|\hat{\theta}_{\{i\}}|+1.96\,\mathrm{se}_{i}, gives a positive gain in determined values. On the pooled HotpotQA log of Section 5.4, it accepts two merges, both of the first kind.

C.3 Retrieval

Algorithm 3 implements the rule Eq. (8). It keeps one counter per memory, and its only state across episodes is the vector of counts 𝐟⁡(t)\mathbf{f}(t).

In the experiments, 𝒦={3,5,8}\mathcal{K}=\{3,5,8\}, M=20M=20 and ρ=0.4\rho=0.4, so ℓt=1,2,3\ell_{t}=1,2,3 at kt=3,5,8k_{t}=3,5,8; the code calls the rule aopt0.4 and the window M_CAND. The size ktk_{t} is drawn uniformly from 𝒦\mathcal{K} by a generator seeded with the seed, the question and the pass, shared by every rule compared in Section 5.3, so the rules differ only in which memories they retrieve. Ties in fi​(t)f_{i}(t) are broken in a fixed order that the sort determines. The rule reads the past only through 𝐟⁡(t)\mathbf{f}(t), a function of 𝐗\mathbf{X}, so it satisfies the condition of Proposition 3. Because the counts change from pass to pass, one query retrieves different sets over time, which breaks the nesting of Lemma B.2.

C.4 The baseline test and costs

The baseline test (Definition A.6) solves 𝐗𝐰=𝟏T\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{1}_{T} by least squares and reports the residual ‖𝐗​𝐰^−𝟏T‖\|\mathbf{X}\hat{\mathbf{w}}-\mathbf{1}_{T}\|. A residual at the level of rounding, such as 3.1×10−153.1\times 10^{-15} on pooled HotpotQA under deterministic top-kk, means that 𝟏T\mathbf{1}_{T} lies in range​𝐗\mathrm{range}\,\mathbf{X} and the log contains a change like 𝐡∅\mathbf{h}_{\emptyset}.

Table 3 gives the cost of each step, with k¯=1T​∑t|St|\bar{k}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}|S_{t}| and pd=∑ℓ≤d(nℓ)p_{d}=\sum_{\ell\leq d}\binom{n}{\ell}. Building 𝐌\mathbf{M} touches each pair of memories in each retrieved set once, which is why its cost depends on k¯\bar{k} and not on nn.

The cubic step dominates. On pooled HotpotQA, with n=2,971n=2{,}971, it is one eigendecomposition of a 2,972×2,9722{,}972\times 2{,}972 matrix. Merging reads each retrieval once, since the history of mim_{i} is the list of episodes that retrieved it; this is the O⁡(n​T)O(nT) bound of Section 4 for a dense representation of 𝐗\mathbf{X}, and O⁡(T​k¯+n)O(T\bar{k}+n) for the sparse one.

Appendix D Experimental Setup

This appendix specifies every experiment of Section 5: the corpora and stores (Appendix D.1), retrieval and reading (Appendix D.2), the retrieval rules (Appendix D.3), the synthetic logs (Appendix D.4), and the statistics (Appendix D.5). Table 4 maps each number in the main text to the run that produces it. The audit of fourteen benchmarks has its own protocol, given in Appendix E.

D.1 Corpora and stores

The retrieval experiments use three corpora with different structure.

HotpotQA.

Each question of HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) comes with ten paragraphs, two of which support the answer. We use the paragraphs as memories and pool the paragraphs of many questions into one shared store, so that a paragraph of one question can be retrieved for another. A few validation items ship fewer than ten paragraphs, and we do not de-duplicate, so 300300 questions give n=2,971n=2{,}971 memories. The gold memories of a question are its supporting paragraphs.

LongMemEval.

Each question of LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2025) comes with a chat history. We use its turns as memories and pool the histories of the questions into one shared store. We use the oracle split. The gold memories of a question are its turns flagged has answer; the accuracy comparison uses the 479479 of 500500 questions that have at least one such turn.

LoCoMo.

LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024) contains long conversations, each with its own questions. We use the turns of a conversation as memories, and all questions of a conversation share its store; retrieval for a question is restricted to its conversation. The gold memories of a question are the turns cited as its evidence. 9 of the 1,5421{,}542 questions cite no evidence and are excluded from gold recall.

D.2 Retrieval and reading

Every memory and every question is embedded with the sentence encoder all-MiniLM-L6 v2 (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019), normalised to unit length, so similarity is the cosine of the embeddings. All rules rank memories by this similarity; they differ in which memories of the ranking they retrieve (Appendix D.3). The reader is gemini-2.5-flash-lite at temperature 00, prompted with the question and the retrieved memories in retrieval order, up to 24,00024{,}000 characters. An answer that matches a gold answer exactly after normalization is correct; otherwise the same model, with a fixed judge prompt, decides. Both prompts are released with the code. Two further readers, gemini-3.6-flash and gemini-3.7-flash, are used only to measure the cost of pooling a store on LongMemEval (Appendix F.4). Hosted models cannot be pinned, so accuracies are reproducible in design and not bit for bit; the retrieval logs and every identifiability number regenerate byte for byte from the released inputs.

D.3 Retrieval rules

Four rules are compared in Section 5.3. All four draw the size ktk_{t} of each retrieval from 𝒦={3,5,8}\mathcal{K}=\{3,5,8\} with the same seeded function of the question and the pass, so they differ only in which memories they retrieve.

  • •

    Deterministic top-kk retrieves the ktk_{t} memories most similar to the query.

  • •

    LEDGER applies the rule Eq. (8) with M=20M=20 and ρ=0.4\rho=0.4 (Algorithm 3); the code calls it aopt0.4.

  • •

    ε\varepsilon-greedy replaces, with probability ε\varepsilon, the top-ktk_{t} set by a uniformly random ktk_{t}-subset of the whole store; we use ε∈{0.1,0.3}\varepsilon\in\{0.1,0.3\}.

  • •

    Score perturbation adds independent Gumbel noise of scale β\beta to each similarity and retrieves the top ktk_{t} of the perturbed scores; we use β∈{0.05,0.10}\beta\in\{0.05,0.10\}.

LEDGER’s sets fall below the drawn size when LtL_{t} and HtH_{t} overlap. On pooled HotpotQA this happens in 1.0%1.0\%, 3.3%3.3\% and 15.9%15.9\% of episodes at kt=3k_{t}=3, 55 and 88, for a mean size of 5.255.25 against 5.335.33 for the other rules, whose sets always have size ktk_{t}. The realized sizes take at least three distinct values, so Proposition 1 is satisfied at d=1d=1 and d=2d=2. The LoCoMo merging run of Section 5.4 uses score perturbation with β=0.08\beta=0.08.

D.4 Synthetic logs

Coverage requires the true values, so the intervals are tested on synthetic logs drawn from the model Eq. (2). A setting fixes the number of memories n∈{10,30}n\in\{10,30\}, the retrieval size k∈{3,5}k\in\{3,5\}, the ratio T/n∈{2,10,50}T/n\in\{2,10,50\} and the ridge parameter λ∈{10−4,10−2,10−1}\lambda\in\{10^{-4},10^{-2},10^{-1}\}, which gives 3636 settings at each resolution d∈{1,2}d\in\{1,2\}. For each setting we draw 2020 random designs and, for each design, 100100 noise vectors, and we record whether every interval that Algorithm 1 reports contains its true value. Joint coverage is the fraction of the 2,0002{,}000 draws in which all reported intervals do. Each design draws, for every episode, a size uniformly from {1,…,k}\{1,\dots,k\} and a uniformly random set of that size, so kk is the largest size. The dividends are independent standard normal, and the noise is standard normal with σ=1\sigma=1, which the interval is given. At d=1d=1 every design has full rank; at d=2d=2, 2424 of the 3636 settings give rank-deficient designs. The restriction of coverage to reported values (Section 5.4) is a post hoc analysis of the same draws; Appendix G records it as such.

The baselines of the width comparison are the pointwise Gaussian interval, which uses the true σ\sigma and no multiplicity correction, and the self-normalised confidence set of Abbasi-Yadkori et al. (2011), evaluated at λ=1\lambda=1 on a separate grid of nn, kk and TT (Appendix F).

D.5 Statistics

Every accuracy comparison is paired: two rules answer the same questions, and we report the mean difference in accuracy with a 95%95\% interval computed by 10,00010{,}000 paired bootstrap resamples over questions (percentile interval) and a two-sided paired permutation test with 10,00010{,}000 sign flips. The four comparisons against the random rules share a family and are Holm-corrected. Fractions determined on pooled HotpotQA are averaged over five seeds (00 to 44), with a range across seeds reported in Appendix F. Every claim with a decision rule was pre-registered before its measurement; Appendix G lists the pre-registered claims, the three that were withdrawn, and the one post hoc analysis.

D.6 Runs behind the main text

Compute.

All identifiability computations, merging and synthetic experiments run on a CPU; the largest step is one eigendecomposition of a 2,972×2,9722{,}972\times 2{,}972 matrix per log. Reader and judge calls go to hosted APIs; the number of calls per experiment is not logged per run; the per-row records account for at least 16,74216{,}742 reader calls.

Appendix E Benchmark Audit

This appendix gives the protocol of the audit in Section 5.2 (Appendix E.1), proves that every one of its 5555 configurations determines no memory value (Appendix E.2), and describes each benchmark (Appendix E.3).

E.1 Protocol

For each benchmark, we build its store as the benchmark specifies and run its retrieval once over its questions, one episode per question, at each retrieval size it uses. We add the sizes 33, 55 and 1010, at the size it specifies where that differs, and at all for the four long-context benchmarks. Each configuration gives a log S1,…,STS_{1},\dots,S_{T}, from which we build 𝐗1\mathbf{X}_{1} and test every memory with Algorithm 1 at d=1d=1, with the baseline column included. We also compute the blocks of the log (Definition A.5), the mean retrieval size, and the number of memories never retrieved. The audit uses the retrieved sets and no outcome, so it calls no reader: by Appendix A.1, whether a value is determined does not depend on the outcomes. By Lemma B.3, a memory undetermined at d=1d=1 is undetermined at every dd, so the audit covers every resolution.

E.2 Why every configuration determines nothing

The audit finds no determined value in any of the 5555 configurations (Table 2). The following lemma explains all of them at once. It extends Theorem 1 from one retrieval size to one size per block.

Lemma E.1 (Constant size within each block).

Suppose that, within each block bb of a log, every episode retrieves the same number kbk_{b} of memories. Then no memory is identifiable at any resolution.

Proof.

Define 𝐰∈ℝn\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} by wi=1/kbw_{i}=1/k_{b} for every memory ii of block bb, and wi=0w_{i}=0 for memories never retrieved. An episode of block bb retrieves kbk_{b} memories, all in block bb, so (𝐗𝐰)t=kb⋅(1/kb)=1(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w})_{t}=k_{b}\cdot(1/k_{b})=1 for every tt. Hence (−1,𝐰)∈ker⁡𝐗1(-1,\mathbf{w})\in\ker\mathbf{X}_{1}, and for every retrieved memory ii the inner product of (0,𝐞i)(0,\mathbf{e}_{i}) with this vector is wi≠0w_{i}\neq 0. A memory never retrieved has a zero column, so (0,𝐞i)∈ker⁡𝐗1(0,\mathbf{e}_{i})\in\ker\mathbf{X}_{1} and its inner product with itself is 11. No memory is identifiable at d=1d=1, and by Lemma B.3 at no higher resolution. ∎

We verified its hypothesis on every one of the 5555 configurations. The hypothesis holds in every configuration of the audit. At a fixed kk, every episode of the log retrieves kk memories. At “all”, every episode of a context retrieves the whole context, so the size is constant within each context, and each block lies within one context. The vector (−1,𝐰)(-1,\mathbf{w}) is a change like 𝐡∅\mathbf{h}_{\emptyset}: it lowers the baseline and raises each memory’s value by the inverse of its block’s retrieval size.

Blocks limit the log further, and would limit it even if the sizes varied. In the six benchmarks with a store per question and one episode per question, every block has Tb=1T_{b}=1, so by Proposition 2 at most one value per question could be determined, whatever the retrieval. The larger HotpotQA run, with 1,2001{,}200 questions, confirms that more questions do not help: the number of blocks grows with the number of questions, and every block still has one episode. The two benchmarks with a shared store, MultiHopRAG and HELMET, split into fewer and larger blocks: MultiHopRAG from 269269 blocks at k=3k=3 to 1515 at k=10k=10, and HELMET into 4141 blocks of 8.78.7 episodes on average at every kk. Their blocks have several episodes each, and the fixed size alone leaves every value undetermined. A shared store is therefore necessary and not sufficient, as Section 5.2 states.

Table 5 gives, for each benchmark, the unit we use as a memory, the scope of its store and the retrieval sizes of the audit. The size the benchmark itself specifies is in bold. The counts TT, nn and the blocks are in Table 2.

Three details affect the counts. In HotpotQA, n=2,971n=2{,}971 for 300300 questions because a few validation items ship fewer than ten paragraphs; at k=10k=10, every paragraph of a question is retrieved. In the “all” configurations, the log keeps TT equal to the number of questions and changes only the retrieval size, whose mean is 104.0104.0 for BABILong, 942.4942.4 for InfiniteBench, 125.5125.5 for QuALITY and 1,372.51{,}372.5 for NarrativeQA on the full text. The HELMET store is capped at 40,00040{,}000 passages by us, for compute.

Table 8 gives the split of Figure 3. On pooled HotpotQA, top-kk retrieves 0.930.93 of the gold memories, and LEDGER lowers the number of gold memories retrieved per question from 2.0002.000 to 1.7581.758 on questions where top-kk retrieved both.

The pre-registered query-time substitute applies LEDGER when the query’s top-11 similarity is below its median over the 1,6001{,}600 questions, 0.6470.647. It changes accuracy by −1.3-1.3 points ([−2.6,−0.1][-2.6,-0.1]) against top-kk and by +1.25+1.25 ([0.0,+2.4][0.0,+2.4]) against ungated LEDGER, and determines 0.5200.520 of the memories. The pre-registered rule required the second interval to exclude zero, so the gate does not transfer the oracle’s result (Appendix G).

F.4 Pooling across readers

Table 9 repeats the comparison of LEDGER and top-kk on pooled HotpotQA with two further readers. The retrieval logs, and therefore every fraction determined, are the same for all readers; only the accuracies change.

F.5 Intervals

Table 10 gives joint coverage at δ=0.05\delta=0.05 on the synthetic logs of Appendix D.4, as the minimum over settings. Coverage over every memory counts the intervals of undetermined memories, which LEDGER does not report; coverage over reported values counts only the intervals that Algorithm 1 returns.

In the 1818 rank-deficient settings that report nothing, every memory of every design is undetermined. Their coverage over every memory ranges down to 0.5720.572, and adding the exact ridge-bias term of Proposition 3, which needs the true 𝜽\bm{\theta}, raises the minimum over all 3636 settings at d=2d=2 to 0.9920.992. This confirms the explanation of Appendix B.7: the undercoverage comes from the part 𝐜2⊤​𝜽\mathbf{c}_{2}^{\!\top}\bm{\theta} of undetermined values. The coverage of a design does not predict whether it reports: one rank-deficient setting (n=30n=30, k=3k=3, T=300T=300) has coverage 0.9760.976 over every memory and reports nothing, because every memory there has a component in the kernel. A separate grid at λ=1\lambda=1 contains one rank-deficient design at d=1d=1, with coverage 0.9640.964 over 20,00020{,}000 draws.

Table 11 compares widths. LEDGER’s interval is close to the pointwise Gaussian interval that knows σ\sigma; the self-normalised confidence set is several times wider at d=1d=1 and an order of magnitude wider at d=2d=2, because its width grows with the number of dividends.

F.6 Merging

Table 12 gives the merging results on pooled HotpotQA with 100100 questions over 2424 passes (n=992n=992, T=2,400T=2{,}400), for two retrieval rules. Fractions are over memories before merging and over units after it.

Merging identical histories removes 123123 units under LEDGER and 2828 under score perturbation, which ties fewer memories. Merging similar histories, with candidates that differ in at most eight episodes, accepts two merges under LEDGER and none under perturbation. On LoCoMo, after three passes of score perturbation with β=0.08\beta=0.08, 79.0%79.0\% of the memories are determined, and merging raises this to 95.7%95.7\% of the units, both estimated on 300300 randomly sampled columns.

F.7 Uses of the determined values

Value recovery.

On synthetic logs with 4040 memories and T=4,000T=4{,}000, over 3030 seeds, the Spearman correlation with the true Shapley values is 0.8920.892 for LEDGER on the 3131 memories it reports, 0.8040.804 when LEDGER splits each group total equally to score all 4040, 0.7240.724 for reward averaging and 0.1180.118 for retrieval frequency.

Retention under a budget.

Ranking undetermined memories last and keeping 30%30\% of the store, the retained store succeeds in 5.525.52 of 300300 evaluation episodes under LEDGER, 6.556.55 under the equal split, 7.147.14 under reward averaging and 6.486.48 under the true Shapley values; the pre-registered real-data retention test was not completed.

Appendix G Pre-registration and Corrections

This appendix records how the empirical claims were tested: which were pre-registered and with what decision rule (Appendix G.1), which were withdrawn (Appendix G.2), the one analysis that was not pre-registered (Appendix G.3), an amendment on the name of the retrieval rule (Appendix G.4), and the defects we found in our own pipeline with the values they changed (Appendix G.5). The dated documents are in the preregistration/ directory of the released code, and the errata in docs/errata.md.

G.1 Pre-registered claims

Before each measurement, we recorded the claim, the quantity that tests it and the rule that decides it, in a dated document committed to the repository. Table 13 lists the claims and their outcomes. A claim holds when its measured quantity, with its interval, satisfies the rule; otherwise it is withdrawn and reported as such.

G.2 Withdrawn claims

Three pre-registered claims were withdrawn because their measured values did not meet their decision rules. We report each with the value it was measured at.

  1. 1.

    Instrumentation is approximately free. The rule required the interval on LEDGER’s accuracy change against top-kk to contain zero with a half-width below 0.0250.025. On 1,6001{,}600 questions of pooled HotpotQA the change is −2.6-2.6 points ([−4.2,−0.9][-4.2,-0.9], permutation p=0.004p=0.004), so the paper reports a cost (Section 5.3).

  2. 2.

    The cost of pooling grows with reader quality. The rule required the pairwise differences between readers to exclude zero. The costs are 15.715.7, 21.021.0 and 19.719.7 points, and two of the three pairwise intervals contain zero (Appendix F.4).

  3. 3.

    The sample-complexity bound. Validation check V7 required the fitted slope of the error against the bound to be at least 1.001.00; it is 0.820.82, which is why 2121 of the 2222 checks pass.

Four further pre-registered tests had negative or incomplete outcomes and are reported in Table 13: the remedy on three audited benchmarks, the reach ceiling, the label-free gate and the retention comparison. The gate was pre-registered as a query-time substitute for the oracle of Section 5.3. It applies LEDGER when the query’s top-11 similarity is below its median, and it did not transfer the oracle’s result (Appendix F.3).

G.3 The post hoc analysis

One result in the paper was not pre-registered: joint coverage restricted to the values that LEDGER reports (Section 5.4 and Table 10). The pre-registered coverage test counted the intervals of every memory, including undetermined ones that LEDGER does not report, and at d=2d=2 it fell to 0.5720.572 on rank-deficient designs. After seeing this, we restricted coverage to the reported values, which gives a minimum of 0.9940.994 over all 3636 settings at d=2d=2. The restriction was chosen after the failure was observed, so it is an analysis and not a test. It uses the same seeds, settings and draws as the pre-registered test, whose numbers are unchanged. Its script and output are released separately from the pre-registeredchecks, and the errata record it as post hoc with its date.

G.4 Amendment on the retrieval rule

One pre-registration document describes LEDGER’s retrieval rule as AA-optimal tie-breaking. The rule that was run is Eq. (8): it fills max⁡(1,round⁡(ρ​kt))\max(1,\mathrm{round}(\rho k_{t})) places with the least-retrieved of the MM most similar memories and the rest by similarity. It is motivated by AA-optimal design (Appendix A.5) and optimises no criterion, and we did not compare it with an AA-optimal choice. The pre-registration is left verbatim, and a dated amendment records this; the name is the only thing at issue, and no number changes. The code and its artifacts keep the label aopt0.4 for this rule.

G.5 Errata

Table 14 lists the defects we found in our pipeline and in the reporting of its results, with the values they affected. Every value in the main text is the corrected one.

Appendix H Discussion

H.1 Interpreting the results

What the results add to estimability.

The condition that decides identifiability is classical: a linear functional 𝐜⊤​𝜽\mathbf{c}^{\!\top}\bm{\theta} is estimable exactly when 𝐜\mathbf{c} lies in the row space of the design matrix (Rao, 1973). The paper adds three things. First, for a retrieval log the design is determined by the retrieved sets, and its Gram matrix at d=1d=1 consists of the retrieval counts Eq. (3), so the condition can be checked from counts that every agent already records. Second, the structure of these counts under common conventions forces specific invisible changes. A fixed retrieval size places 𝐡B\mathbf{h}_{B} in ker⁡𝐗d\ker\mathbf{X}_{d} for every |B|<d|B|<d (Theorem 1). Since (𝐜(i))⊤​𝐡∅=1(\mathbf{c}^{(i)})^{\!\top}\mathbf{h}_{\emptyset}=1 for every memory at d=1d=1, no memory is identifiable at any number of episodes. For binary outcomes the conclusion is stronger than the absence of an unbiased linear estimator: the distribution of the log is the same for two different values of φi\varphi_{i}, so no estimator is consistent. Third, the condition fails on every one of the 5555 configurations of fourteen standard benchmarks (Table 2). Methods that assign a value to every memory therefore report, on these logs, numbers that the solver chooses and the data do not constrain. Slate off-policy evaluation works with the same counts and sets the undetermined part aside, because it does not change the value of a policy (Swaminathan et al., 2017); for memory valuation, the undetermined part names the memories that cannot be valued.

Why Shapley values and Möbius dividends.

The Shapley value is the unique attribution that satisfies efficiency, symmetry, null player and additivity (Shapley, 1953), and it is the notion used by attribution-based memory systems (Wei et al., 2026b; Ye and Yoganarasimhan, 2025; Patel et al., 2025). Writing vv in dividends makes the expected outcome of each episode linear in 𝜽\bm{\theta} and makes each value a linear functional (𝐜(i))⊤​𝜽(\mathbf{c}^{(i)})^{\!\top}\bm{\theta}, which is what turns valuation into a question about the row space of 𝐗d\mathbf{X}_{d}. The same test applies to any value that is linear in 𝜽\bm{\theta}, with its own coefficient vector. The Banzhaf value (Banzhaf III, 1964), for example, is ∑B∋i21−|B|​θB\sum_{B\ni i}2^{1-|B|}\theta_{B}. At d=1d=1 the choice does not matter: every marginal contribution v⁡(S∪{i})−v⁡(S)v(S\cup\{i\})-v(S) equals θ{i}\theta_{\{i\}}, so every probabilistic value (Weber, 1988) of memory ii equals θ{i}\theta_{\{i\}}, and our results at d=1d=1 hold for all of them.

Resolution.

The experiments on real logs test identifiability at d=1d=1, and this suffices for the audit. If 𝐡∈ker⁡𝐗d\mathbf{h}\in\ker\mathbf{X}_{d} and (𝐜(i))⊤​𝐡≠0(\mathbf{c}^{(i)})^{\!\top}\mathbf{h}\neq 0, extending 𝐡\mathbf{h} by zeros on the columns of order d+1d+1 gives a vector in ker⁡𝐗d+1\ker\mathbf{X}_{d+1}, and its inner product with the coefficients of φi\varphi_{i} at resolution d+1d+1 is the same nonzero number, because the two coefficient vectors agree on sets of size at most dd. A memory undetermined at resolution dd is therefore undetermined at every higher resolution, and the 5555 configurations determine no value at any dd. The positive results use d=1d=1 for a different reason. The design 𝐗d\mathbf{X}_{d} has pd=∑ℓ=0d(nℓ)p_{d}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{d}\binom{n}{\ell} columns and rank at most TT, and the log needs at least d+1d+1 distinct retrieval sizes (Proposition 1); at d=2d=2 and n=2,971n=2{,}971, p2≈4.4×106p_{2}\approx 4.4\times 10^{6}, far above T=7,200T=7{,}200. We therefore study d=2d=2 on synthetic logs only (Section 5.4). What d=1d=1 omits is bounded by Proposition A.1: |φi​(v)−φi​(v(1))|≤12​∑B∋i,|B|>1|θB||\varphi_{i}(v)-\varphi_{i}(v^{(1)})|\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{B\ni i,\,|B|>1}|\theta_{B}|.

Associational and causal values.

Identifiability depends on 𝐗d\mathbf{X}_{d} alone, and so do all results of Section 3. Estimation depends also on the noise. Writing vq=v+δqv_{q}=v+\delta_{q}, the noise of the linear model is εt=ηt+δqt​(St)\varepsilon_{t}=\eta_{t}+\delta_{q_{t}}(S_{t}), and because retrieval reads the query, δqt​(St)\delta_{q_{t}}(S_{t}) can correlate with the design. The estimates then describe the log: they equal the dividends of vv when the log is exogenous (Definition A.3), for example when StS_{t} is independent of qtq_{t}, and they can be biased otherwise. Appending query features to the design removes the part of 𝜹\bm{\delta} in their span and leaves every result on identifiability unchanged, since appending columns never makes a non-estimable functional estimable (Appendix A.3). A separate condition concerns adaptivity: Proposition 3 requires that the retrieved sets do not depend on past outcomes. LEDGER’s rule Eq. (8) depends on the past only through the counts fi​(t)f_{i}(t), which are functions of 𝐗\mathbf{X}, so it satisfies this condition.

Random retrieval.

Randomising retrieval also breaks the nesting of top-kk, and at high enough rates ε\varepsilon-greedy and score perturbation determine more values than LEDGER (Figure 3a). They draw replacements from the whole store, so the reader loses evidence: reaching a fraction of 0.980.98 or more costs them between 13.313.3 and 37.037.0 accuracy points. LEDGER draws its replacements from the MM memories most similar to the query and keeps the most similar ones in HtH_{t}, which bounds how much evidence it can displace.

The accuracy cost.

LEDGER’s effect on accuracy ranges from −2.6-2.6 points on HotpotQA to +2.7+2.7 on LoCoMo and falls as the gold recall of top-kk rises (Figure 3b). Its mechanism is displacement: the loss comes from questions where top-kk had already retrieved every gold memory (Figure 3c). Where top-kk misses evidence, spreading retrieval costs nothing measurable, and an oracle that applies LEDGER only there keeps 64%64\% of the gain with no measurable loss. The pre-registered query-time substitute, top-11 similarity, did not reproduce this result (Appendix F).

H.2 Scope and open problems

Scope.

The analysis uses three properties of the setting: in each episode a system chooses a set of items from a pool, it observes one scalar outcome, and the expected outcome is a sum of dividends of order at most dd. It does not use the fact that the items are memories. The same test therefore applies to the tools an agent calls in an episode, the passages a retrieval-augmented generator reads, and the slates a recommender shows (Swaminathan et al., 2017), and each of these settings has its own versions of the fixed size, the private pool and the tied items.

A query-time gate.

The oracle of Section 5.3 shows that most of the gain is available without cost when LEDGER is applied only to questions where top-kk misses evidence. A deployed agent has no gold labels, and the first substitute we pre-registered failed. A gate that predicts, at query time, whether top-kk has found the evidence would make this trade available in deployment.

An exact optimal-design rule.

LEDGER’s rule Eq. (8) targets the diagonal of 𝐕−1\mathbf{V}^{-1} through retrieval counts, using (𝐕−1)i​i≥1/Vi​i(\mathbf{V}^{-1})_{ii}\geq 1/V_{ii}. The AA-optimal choice (Pukelsheim, 2006) among sets drawn from RtR_{t} would maximise the reduction in tr⁡(𝐕−1)\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{V}^{-1}), which by the Sherman–Morrison identity is ‖𝐕−1​𝐱S‖2/(1+𝐱S⊤​𝐕−1​𝐱S)\|\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{S}\|^{2}/(1+\mathbf{x}_{S}^{\!\top}\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{S}) for a set with row 𝐱S\mathbf{x}_{S}. A greedy search over RtR_{t} costs O⁡(M​kt​pd)O(Mk_{t}p_{d}) per episode given 𝐕−1\mathbf{V}^{-1}, and a rank-one update of 𝐕−1\mathbf{V}^{-1} costs O⁡(pd2)O(p_{d}^{2}). Whether it determines more values than the count-based rule, and at what cost in accuracy, is open.

Higher resolution.

At d≥2d\geq 2, the number of dividends grows as ndn^{d}, and most values need TT of the same order to be determined. If only a few dividends of order two are nonzero, identifiability becomes a question of sparse recovery, whose conditions on 𝐗d\mathbf{X}_{d} differ from the row-space condition used here.

Other outcome models.

For a binary outcome with an invertible link gg, 𝔼⁡[rt]=g−1​((𝐗d​𝜽)t)\mathbb{E}[r_{t}]=g^{-1}\bigl((\mathbf{X}_{d}\bm{\theta})_{t}\bigr), the distribution of the log determines 𝐗d​𝜽\mathbf{X}_{d}\bm{\theta}, so the row-space condition and every result of Section 3 carry over unchanged. The dividends then describe the value on the scale of the link, and the estimator and its intervals would need to change.

Adaptive and changing stores.

Rules that choose sets from past outcomes, such as bandit algorithms, violate the condition of Proposition 3. Intervals that remain valid under such rules exist, such as the confidence set of Abbasi-Yadkori et al. (2011), but they are 6.66.6 to 3636 times as wide in our synthetic study. A store that grows over time adds columns that start at zero: a new memory is undetermined until it has been retrieved with varied partners and at varied sizes, which gives a natural schedule for when its value can first be reported.

H.3 Applications

Attribution in language models.

Attribution asks which parts of a model’s input or training data an output depends on. Data attribution values training examples by their effect on a trained model (Ghorbani and Zou, 2019), context attribution values the sources in a prompt by their effect on a generation (Cohen-Wang et al., 2024), and Shapley-based methods value the passages of a retrieval-augmented generator (Patel et al., 2025; Ye and Yoganarasimhan, 2025). These methods obtain their evidence by design: they ablate random subsets of the sources and fit a surrogate to the outcomes. A deployed system cannot run such ablations on its own traffic, and when the same estimators are fitted to logged data, they return a number for every source whether or not the log determines it. Our results supply the missing check. Whether a log determines an attribution depends only on the log’s counts, so it can be decided before any attribution is estimated, and it applies to every attribution that is linear in the dividends (Appendix H.1). The results also explain why designed ablations succeed: independent random subsets vary in size and are not nested, so with enough of them 𝐗1\mathbf{X}_{1} has full column rank, while the logs that retrieval produces under a fixed size have a nonzero kernel at every TT (Theorem 1).

Cognitive models of memory.

The rational analysis of human memory holds that the availability of a memory tracks the probability that it will be needed, which the environment reveals through the frequency and recency of past use (Anderson and Schooler, 1991). Agent memory systems adopted these signals directly: they score memories by recency, importance and relevance (Park et al., 2023), decay them along a forgetting curve (Zhong et al., 2024), or rank them by access frequency (Wei et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2026a). Frequency and recency measure how often a memory is needed. They do not measure how much a memory contributes to the outcome when it is retrieved, and a store managed for an agent needs both. Our results separate the two quantities within one object. The retrieval frequencies are the diagonal of 𝐗⊤​𝐗\mathbf{X}^{\!\top}\mathbf{X} Eq. (1), so they are exactly what a log records about need, while the contribution φi\varphi_{i} is a functional of the outcomes. The same counts decide whether the contribution can be learned: a memory retrieved in every episode of a top-kk log has the largest frequency and an undetermined value (Theorem 1). A model of agent memory built on need alone therefore cannot tell a frequently retrieved memory that helps from one that is only retrieved often, and LEDGER supplies the missing quantity where the log determines it.

Human control of personal memory.

Assistants with persistent memory store facts about their users across conversations. Users value the personalization this brings, and they ask for transparent control over what is stored and for accurate memories (Chen et al., 2026a). Control requires knowing which memories matter. Research on human–AI decision-making shows that people should rely on a system’s advice only when it is correct (Schemmer et al., 2023), and that over-reliance on incorrect advice resists simple remedies such as explanations (Buçinca et al., 2021). A user deciding whether to delete, correct or keep a memory relies on the system’s account of that memory, and current systems show what is stored without any statement of what each memory does. LEDGER gives each memory one of two answers that a user can rely on. A determined value comes with a confidence interval, so its uncertainty is stated. An undetermined value is reported as such, so the system makes no claim that its log cannot support. Merging reduces the store without losing a determined value (Theorem 2), which makes it safe to present fewer, larger units to a user. The same statements identify which memories an agent relies on, which supports profiling as well as control, and they should be governed by the policy that governs the store.

Training memory agents with reinforcement learning.

Reinforcement learning from outcome rewards underlies recent reasoning models (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025), and it now trains agents to manage memory: which entries to add, update or delete, and which to use in an answer (Yan et al., 2026b). Related methods learn a value for each memory from downstream reward (Tan et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026). Every such method faces a credit-assignment problem: the reward belongs to the episode, and the value of each memory must be inferred from which memories the episode retrieved. This is the inverse problem of this paper, with the rollouts as the log and the reward as the outcome. When rollouts retrieve a fixed number of memories, the rewards leave every memory’s credit undetermined (Theorem 1), so a learned per-memory value is fixed by the learner and not by the rewards; co-retrieved memories then receive spurious credit (Yang et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2026a). Our test applies to the rollout log before training, because it reads only which memories each rollout retrieved. LEDGER’s retrieval makes rollouts that determine more values, and its determined values, with their intervals, can serve as per-memory rewards that no undetermined memory receives. Rollout policies that adapt to past rewards violate the condition of Proposition 3, so their intervals need the wider self-normalized bounds of Abbasi-Yadkori et al. (2011); identifiability is unaffected, since it depends on 𝐗d\mathbf{X}_{d} alone.

Evaluating memory systems.

Memory benchmarks have moved from single questions to long conversations and multi-session interactions, and from answer accuracy toward the operations a memory system performs over time (Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026). They still score a memory system by the answers it produces. None of them can score its valuation, because none of them provides ground truth for the value of a memory, and their own protocols leave every value undetermined (Table 2). Our results provide ground truth of two kinds. Whether a value is determined is a theorem about the log, so a benchmark can report the fraction of values its logs determine alongside accuracy, and a valuation method can be tested on whether it abstains exactly on the undetermined memories. Where a value is determined, synthetic logs with known dividends test its interval, as in Section 5.4. The changes a benchmark needs are small and are all changes to its protocol: a shared store, several retrieval sizes and several passes per question.

H.4 Limitations

Model.

The results assume that the query-averaged value has no dividends above order dd (Assumption 2), and the real-data experiments use d=1d=1. Omitted dividends bias the estimates wherever they correlate with the design, and Proposition A.1 bounds only their direct effect on each value. The noise is assumed conditionally sub-Gaussian (Assumption 1). The reported values are associational unless the log is exogenous (Appendix H.1).

Estimation.

Coverage of the intervals is measured on synthetic logs drawn from the model, where the true values are known; on real logs it cannot be measured. The result that coverage holds on every reported value at d=2d=2 comes from a post hoc analysis (Appendix G). The interval in Eq. (5) omits the ridge-bias term of Proposition 3, which is small for λ=10−2\lambda=10^{-2} on the values LEDGER reports and is the cause of undercoverage on values it does not report.

Retrieval.

LEDGER’s rule is a count-based heuristic motivated by AA-optimal design; it optimises no criterion. Its sets fall below the drawn size in 6.7%6.7\% of episodes on pooled HotpotQA (Appendix D). The rule treats the M=20M=20 memories most similar to the query as candidates of comparable relevance, and we did not test this assumption directly. Its effect on accuracy depends on the corpus, from −2.6-2.6 to +2.7+2.7 points, and the only rule that removes the cost is an oracle that needs gold labels.

Experiments.

The accuracy experiments use hosted readers that cannot be pinned and a single judge model, so they are reproducible in design and not bit for bit. The pooled stores for HotpotQA and LongMemEval are our construction; the benchmarks define private stores. The audit runs each benchmark at one pass. The LoCoMo merging result uses score perturbation, not LEDGER’s rule, on three conversations, with fractions estimated on 300300 sampled columns. The random rules’ accuracy is measured on 300300 questions, and LEDGER’s on 1,6001{,}600.
